Subject: [ballyalley] BalZerk Version 00002


























      Room generation now working!



Long story,



When I started with the scroll demo, I was originally thinking of having 

a set number of rooms stored on cart, or generating it from reading code...



It made sense to me to build the room by walls rather than by spaces/sub

rooms as there were less of them and I could use bit patterns to control

them.



However, a good enough way to make proper rooms escaped me.



I briefly talked with a guy who had made a BerZerk clone for the C64. He

was using a Maze generation routine that divided the Room/maze into

smaller spaces/Sub rooms and checked if you could get to a room from an

adjoining room.



It seemed like a big and cumbersome solution, but a workable one.

However, I remembered seeing rooms with a box in the middle. So I asked

about that and he admitted he had to fudge the routine to get that type

of room to show up.



So, I let it sit there. Occasionally looking for a better solution.



Then I found this:



http://www.robotron2084guidebook.com/home/games/berzerk/mazegenerator/code/



I was stunned! I was closer worrying about the walls rather than the

spaces, but it never occurred to me to even look at the pillars of the

walls!



The actual arcade basically spins a single wall around each of the 8

pillars that line the middle of the room. This easily gives ample

pathways and only occasionally do enough walls position themselves to

make a box in the middle of the room.



I'm not entirely sure my routine is working exactly right, but it looks

good. If it is close enough, it should make approx 870 odd mazes.



The resulting code I think is actually smaller that I was going to have

with my old routine.



Anyway,



For your enjoyment, This version will continuously make rooms and scroll

them off screen. It works great in MESS. I haven't tried it on an actual

Bally/Astrocade yet. I worry it might overheat the video chip with all

that scrolling...

13506:
I added 1983's "Quadra" for expanded BASIC by Mike White.  "Quadra" was archived from identical commercial tapes in Ken Lill's and Richard Houser's tape collections.  You can get the program here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/programs_q-z/programs_q-z.html#QuadraBRB

The tape contained three different variations of the expanded BASIC version of "Quadra" on one tape that contained:
                           
1) "Quadra (Practice Programs)"
2) "Quadra The Ultimate (The Marathon) (4K)"
3) "Quadra The Ultimate (The Marathon) (16K)"

Here are more details about the three different versions of the game:

----------------------------------------

"Quadra (Practice Programs)"

The tape had a menu and six games in this order:

1. Ping
2. Smash-Up
3. Laser Blaster
4. Landslide!
5. Safe Cracker
6. UFO Attack

You should be able to play the tape all the way through and the menu will find the game you select, but I had trouble with this.  It worked fine if I only played the recording of the game I selected.  This doesn't seem all that different from the AstroBASIC version, though there are a few more colors.

----------------------------------------

"Quadra The Ultimate (The Marathon) (4K)"

The first part contains the main menu.  You randomly play one of four games:

1) "Smash-Up"
2) "Laser, & Slide"
3) "UFO Attack"
4) "Safe Cracker".

"Laser,&Slide" is actually a combination of three games--"Laser Blaster", "Brick Buster", and "Avalanche!".

Try to complete each game before losing all of your lives.  The games are divided between the three parts of the program.  Part 1 contains "Smash-Up" in addition to the menu.  Part 2 contains "Laser,&Slide" and "UFO Attack".  Part 3 contains "Safe Cracker".

----------------------------------------

"Quadra The Ultimate (The Marathon) (16K)"

The first part is "Q Cartoon".  Load this first, and wait for the cartoon to finish playing.  Then play the three loads of the second part (no need to pause between these).  This loads the menu and all four quadrants together, so there's no need to reload afterward.  Compared to the 4K version, the menu has some extra effects, and instructions are included this time.  The games themselves seem to play identically.

----------------------------------------

The tape can be viewed here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/cassette_pics/misc/misc.html#QuadraTapeBRB

The docs can be viewed here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/cart_manuals/cart_manuals.html#QuadraDocs

Have fun!

Adam

I added 1982's "2-Letter Music Maker" by Ken Lill.  This AstroBASIC program was printed in ARCADIAN 4, no. 10 (Aug. 06, 1982): 99.  It can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#2-LetterMusicMaker

I've OCRed the instructions from "The Arcadian:"

2-LETTER MUSIC MAKER is another demonstration-type program. This one illustrates the various functions of the music/noise generation system that can be controlled using the two-letter controls of Astro Basic. This program is only AB, of course.

To move the "blinking" box, just move the joystick backwards and forwards [JY(1)]. To select your "notes", use your knob ALONG WITH your trigger [KN(1) & TR(1)] for "course" tuning and let go of the trigger and move your joystick left or right for "fine" tuning. One thing to remember is that the quantity is the same as 255 to the Bally. Typing in "TA=255" uses one byte MORE than typing in "TA=-1"!! To turn off ALL notes and set ALL 2-letter music variables to ZERO, just move the "blinking" box to the "DOWN-ARROW" and squeeze the trigger. This is the same as typing in the "DOWN-ARROW" in your program. One note: the variables in this program are set to only go to the maximum that is used by the 2-letter system.

Line >300 is in the program only as a convenience. It is not necessary to type this line in!!

Paul's brief archiving notes are that this Arcadian program was found in the Bob Fabris Collection and that this version includes a text title screen.

Enjoy!

13512:
Oh, MAN!

Having all the RAM used by screen really makes it hard.

In the scroll demos, I use 96 rows of screen, leaving 6 lines of screen or 6*40 = 240 bytes to use.

However, Berzerk at max has (I've counted) 11 robots sharing 5-7 shots (two different reports...), 1 man with a minimum of 1 shot looks like 2 max...

For a total of 19-21 objects on screen at one time.

I need to see how many objects the Bally/Astrocade can move at a reasonable speed.

The Berzerk arcade does show some slowdown with everything on and speeds up as you destroy robots. But we don't want to be too slow.

Anyway, 19 objects using the standard Vector block takes up:
19 * 15 = 285 bytes.

I decided to stop at 10 robots so 270 bytes... Not counting score, Room number ect...

Now you remember I had 240 bytes to play with. Removing 1 extra line from the display, moving the maze up 1 line, gives me an extra 40 bytes or 280.

Great! right?

Not so fast...

The system ROM uses bytes 4FCE-4FFF for handling the system routines. (And Yes, I remember Don't touch 4FFF)
That's 49 Bytes.
Running my program in MESS with debug on, tells me the STACK is at minimum 4FAA or about... That is 36 Bytes between SP and system variables.

270+49+36=355 bytes needed.

Calculating...
280+40=320+40=360

I need to shrink the screen by 2 more rows. I can lose the player # and just display the score like the arcade. This will allow me to move the maze up two more rows without changing it.

However, I would like to explore other ways of saving space. like using a smaller Vector block (Last two bytes are optional)

Less robots? The current ones are a bit large, as they are the same number of pixels as the arcade, buy the Bally/Astrocade is half the resolution or abouts.

I have also considered shrinking the man and robots to closer sizes to the arcade.

This is the first time I've tried to do anything serious in such a limited system.

Of course, we still have more RAM that the 2600.(128 bytes). If it can do Berzerk, we can do it better. :)

Lance

13516:
These program updates is a fascinating subject, Lance.

To save RAM, maybe it's time to leave the comfort of using the vector movement routines and make your own routines (no small feat, I know).  This might also allow you to make the movement in the game be faster than the vector routines allow.  I think Brett Bilbrey's "Treasure Trove" did this for a similar reason that you're running into now.  You might want to try poking around that game's source code, which is available here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/ml_source.html#TreasureCoveSource

Richard Degler might be able help out; maybe he'll chime in.  Certainly Michael Garber, as Ken has already said, would be able to help you out.  I know that he had to also not use the Vector routines too.  I have the source code for his two games, but he doesn't want it posted online or shared.  Basically, I'm his back-up system.  Maybe you can contact him and ask him to share it with you too?

Keep on making postings like this one.  It also might help to make your posting subjects a bit more specific when you're asking for help.  Maybe something like "Help: Need to Conserve RAM for Homebrew 'BalZerk.'"  The more specific your posting subject, then the more people might take a look at it.

Adam

To: ballyalley@yahoogroups.com
From: ballyalley@yahoogroups.com
Date: Wed, 8 Apr 2015 19:45:04 -0400
Subject: [ballyalley] BalZerk Project Update


























      Oh, MAN!



Having all the RAM used by screen really makes it hard.



In the scroll demos, I use 96 rows of screen, leaving 6 lines of screen

or 6*40 = 240 bytes to use.



However, Berzerk at max has (I've counted) 11 robots sharing 5-7 shots

(two different reports...), 1 man with a minimum of 1 shot looks like 2

max...



For a total of 19-21 objects on screen at one time.



I need to see how many objects the Bally/Astrocade can move at a

reasonable speed.



The Berzerk arcade does show some slowdown with everything on and speeds

up as you destroy robots. But we don't want to be too slow.



Anyway, 19 objects using the standard Vector block takes up:

19 * 15 = 285 bytes.



I decided to stop at 10 robots so 270 bytes... Not counting score, Room

number ect...



Now you remember I had 240 bytes to play with. Removing 1 extra line

from the display, moving the maze up 1 line, gives me an extra 40 bytes

or 280.



Great! right?



Not so fast...



The system ROM uses bytes 4FCE-4FFF for handling the system routines.

(And Yes, I remember Don't touch 4FFF)

That's 49 Bytes.

Running my program in MESS with debug on, tells me the STACK is at

minimum 4FAA or about... That is 36 Bytes between SP and system variables.



270+49+36=355 bytes needed.



Calculating...

280+40=320+40=360



I need to shrink the screen by 2 more rows. I can lose the player # and

just display the score like the arcade. This will allow me to move the

maze up two more rows without changing it.



However, I would like to explore other ways of saving space. like using

a smaller Vector block (Last two bytes are optional)



Less robots? The current ones are a bit large, as they are the same

number of pixels as the arcade, buy the Bally/Astrocade is half the

resolution or abouts.



I have also considered shrinking the man and robots to closer sizes to

the arcade.



This is the first time I've tried to do anything serious in such a

limited system.



Of course, we still have more RAM that the 2600.(128 bytes). If it can

do Berzerk, we can do it better. :)



Lance

13519:
I was watering outside this morning thinking about Lance and his game, "BalZerk."  I wasn't thinking about reducing the RAM required, but rather a way to speed-up movement when the screen gets hectic.  Since there are no sprites on the Bally, all movement is done via software.  This means that the less RAM that has to be moved around by the CPU the faster movement can potentially become.  In this vein, maybe just reducing the robot's size would be helpful.  Then again, the Bally's screen resolution is already extremely limited, so making the robots smaller, and still keep them looking like evil robots out to kill the player might be a good trick to pull off.

Adam

I added a 1981 Bally BASIC demonstration program called "Ward's Display" by Ken Springsteen.

This is a simple demonstration program that Ken Springsteen wrote for use at a Montgomery Ward located near him in the NorthPark Mall in Devanport, Iowa.   The program lists the store's name along with what can be created with the "Bally Home Computer Cartridge" (never referred to as BASIC).  In then lists 23 BASIC programs that, the demo claims, are available for $3 each.

Several Ken Springsteen programs (Crypt-o-grams,
 Spirals Visual, Arcade Visual, and Ward's Display) were on a tape in
the Bob Fabris collection labeled "Ken Springsteen Programs For The
Arcadian."  Crypt-o-grams was published, and I guess the others should
be considered unpublished submissions.

"Ward's Display" can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#WardsDisplayKenSpringsteen

I had a difficult time finding any information about this program until I found a letter that Ken wrote to Bob Fabris in January 1982.  The letter can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#ToBobFabrisFromKenSpringsteenJan021982

Ken wrote a letter to Bob Fabris on January 2, 1982 that has additional information concerning this program.  I absolutely love finding seemingly lost information about unknown programs.  This is what archiving is really all about to me.

The following, which concerns "Ward's Display," is an excerpt from Ken's letter:

In early November I went to the Montgomery Wards at Northpark and offered to give a free demonstration of the Bally Arcade and Basic cartridge. (Astrovision Basic was not available yet.) In the next two weeks I gave three 5-hour demonstrations including programs from the Arcadian and WaveMakers. I also displayed all three volumes of the Arcadian. Now I have the new Basic and I'm going to be giving more demonstrations of old programs converted to Astro-Basic.

Following my demonstrations, Wards was sold out of the arcade for two weeks. Now they give me 10% discount on all arcade accessories. They also give my name and phone number to everyone who buys an arcade and tell them to call me if they have any questions. Several people have called me to ask why the Artillery Duel program in the instruction book won't work. I tell them about the RND that was misspelled in line 430, then I tell them about the Bally user group I'm assembling. Finally I tell them that they should subscribe to the Arcadian, and order all the back issues, to get the most use from their arcade and Basic.

If they ask me about the Basic Express I tell them that all the back issues weren't worth the two month wait after they cashed the check I sent them. I'm still waiting for the Sept.-Oct. issue!!!

Two stores that sell the arcade opened up recently in the Quad Cities but they didn't know the Basic even existed. I am planning on offering to give them demonstrations soon. There are now a total of four stores in the Quad cities that sell the arcade and Videocades: Montgomery Wards (Northpark & Southpark), Video Island (Northpark), and WSTL Home Video (N. Brady St. Davenport). I would be glad to deliver any package of information, about The Arcadian, Astrovision- Basic, or software producers, to all four of these stores.

The Demonstration Information Displayed:

I examined the very simple BASIC code.  When "Ward's Display" is run it shows all of the following information in a well-formatted display on the Bally's screen:

MONTGOMERY WARDS OF NORTHPARK
PRESENTS
THE BALLY PROFESSIONAL ARCADE
AND

WITH THE BALLY HOME COMPUTER CARTRIDGE YOU CAN CREATE YOUR OWN

THE POSSIBILITIES ARE ENDLESS!!

YOU CAN EVEN TRADE GAMES WITH YOUR FRIENDS BY RECORDING THEM ON ANY
BLANK CASETTE TAPE!!

HERE IS A LIST OF JUST A PORTION OF ALL THE GAMES THAT ARE AVAILABLE:

HORSE RACE
MASTERMIND
CONNECT-4
ELLO             <-- Misprint: It probably should say O-Jello.
CHECKERS
BACKGAMMON
OLD BENT NOSE
ENEMY ATTACK
PACK-RAT
SUB HUNTER
SLOT MACHINE
INVASION FORCE
HANG MAN

& SEVERAL MORE (TOO NUMEROUS TO MENTION)

AND ALL AT A COST OF LESS THAN $3.00 PER GAME!!
INTERESTED?
WE'LL BE GLAD TO HELP YOU


After the information is displayed, the program waits a short while with a FOR loop, and then the program re-runs.

Gathering all of this information took quite some time, but it was enjoyable and enlightening.  I hope that you've enjoyed reading and learning about a lost piece of information in the overall Bally Arcade/Astrocade grand puzzle.

Have fun!

I added a Bally BASIC program called "2732 EPROM Programmer" by Perkins Engineering.  The Blue Ram interface with EPROM burner is required.

This program will burn a 4K EPROM using the Blue Ram Interface and its EPROM burner expansion. This program must pre-date the Blue Ram Utility, which includes the ability to burn 2732 and 2764 EPROMs.

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/perkins_engineering/perkins_engineering.html#2732EPROMProgrammer

Load this utility into Bally BASIC with :INPUT. It starts with a machine language driver, and then includes a Bally BASIC program.

The utility requires a Blue RAM expansion and an EPROM burner. Without a compatible EPROM burner, the program could not be fully tested. Nonetheless, it is believed that this was archived correctly. While there was only have a single tape with it, the same results processing two different recordings of it. Paul got no error messages either processing it or loading it. The program displays a menu and behaves sensibly, i.e. if asked to compare the ROM and RAM, it told Paul that they don't match. However, since it is unknown if the program processed correctly, both a digitally archived and RAW version of the software is included.

Paul mentioned that I might want to add some notes and files to the Perkins Engineering drivers from his disassemblies.  Since I never finished with this project, I decline (but it's a good idea).

Enjoy!

Added "Bally Writer" by Clyde Perkins Perkins Engineering.  This Blue Ram BASIC program requires 16K RAM and it loads via the Blue Ram's 2000-baud interface.

This program allows the user to write notes and letters which can be printed.

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/perkins_engineering/perkins_engineering.html#BallyWriterPerkins

Information about this program is limited, but some information about it is available in Mike White's "The Bally Astrocade Hardware Guide: Plans, Prototypes and Production, Incorporating Thorough References to the Classic Newsletters."  You can view that entire guide, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/bally_astrocade_hardware_guide_faq.txt

The following pertinent information has been excerpted from the above guide:

One last (but certainly not least) aspect of the Blue RAM that should be mentioned is its success in being interfaced with an NEC PC-8023A-C Dot-Matrix Impact Printer (122)!  This enabled portions of the newsletters themselves to be done with the Arcade!  Exactly how much is unclear, but four programs ("The Listing Formatter," "Bally Writer" by Clyde Perkins, "Snoop Camera" and a right-justifying "Word Processor" by Don Gladden and Ken Lill) (123) were responsible for quite a bit of productivity!  For just one example, the "Word Processor" enabled Mike White to compose the tutorial series "Tricks of the Trade" (124).  Three of the programs mentioned above were even modified to take advantage of the NEC control commands shown on page 152 of the fifth Arcadian!

A modified version of "The Listing Formatter," called "The Lister," appeared on page 87 of the seventh Arcadian and is known to have done a few of the newsletter's listings.


Here are the footnotes for the above two paragraphs:

Finally, I've OCRed  part of the "Blue Ram Modem Interface (with optional Printer Port) Owner's Manual."  This excerpt explains how to operate the modem with the Blue Ram Modem/Printer Interface:


When the program tape is loaded, it will display a menu of functions on the screen. Use the keyboard to select the desired function (a RETURN is not necessary). If function 1 is selected, the modem functions are bypassed and the keyboard and printer are configured as a "typewriter." What is typed on the keyboard will be printed on the screen and on the printer when the RETURN key is pressed. Use CNTL H (hold the CNTL key and press the capital H) to make a backspace (erase). This will print a ? on the screen but will erase one character in the printer's memory. You may use any of the programming functions of the 800B printer (see Table 4-1 and 4-2). For example, pressing ESC followed by : will set the automatic form-feed mode to skip the paper to the top of the next form. Similarly you may use CNTL L to feed a form immediately. Note that the left blank key on the keyboard may be used to switch to bold print and back to normal print again.

Press any key on the keypad to return to the function menu.

If function 2 is selected (normal communications function), the program is configured as a "dumb terminal" which transmits all keyboard characters and displays all characters received from the modem. If the printer is online, a hard copy is automatically made of all data received. Use of the printer is optional here.

Function 3 is similar to function 2 except that no screen display occurs. This mode is useful when a long message is being received for hard copy. The printer will run faster when screen output is suppressed. To use this mode, select function 2 first to begin the dialogue and request the data. Then press the keypad to return to the menu and select function 3 to suppress screen output. Note that this technique of function switching can be used to program the printer for auto form-feed, etc. using function 1 and then return to the function menu and select function 2 for normal communications.

Function 4 allows up to 3072 characters to be repeated for display and/or printing. When the program asks "HOW MANY CHARACTERS?" enter a number from 0 to 3071 and press RETURN. This tells the program how many characters you want repeated. A zero entry tells the program to repeat all characters from the beginning of this block of 3072. For example, if 5100 characters had been received, the current block contains only the last 28 characters (5100-3072). Therefore, an entry of zero in this case would cause the last 28 characters to be repeated. An entry of 500 would cause the last 500 characters to be repeated. If 500 characters had not been received, garbled text will print and/or display for the characters not received. One valuable use of the repeat function is automatic duplication of a "typed" page using the zero entry.

Be sure to include a form-feed at the end of the text to prevent the duplicate from beginning on the same page.

Additional Notes:

1. With the CAPS LOCK key latched down, all letter keys are typed as capitals and the SHIFT key shifts the letter keys to lower case. With the CAPS LOCK key up, all letter keys are typed in lower case and the SHIFT key shifts the letter keys to capitals. CAPS LOCK only affects the letter keys.

2. Communications protocols vary widely from network to network. Consult the applicable network documentation for the proper sign-on sequence.

3. If you are a member of the Source, please feel free to leave us mail messages addressed to TCV403.

Notes from Ken Lill:

John Perkins kept on refining the "Blue Ram Utility" and adding new features. Then, in the 2000s, Ken Lill altered the program; he changed one byte so that it would run on a non-Blue Ram extended memory unit, such as the Lil' WHITE RAM or the 64KRAM board. It still had a major problem testing the RAM memory of non-Blue Ram units correctly. Ken modified his version so that it will check ANY add-on unit as long as it has contiguous memory from 8000H. It will stop checking when there is no memory or if a bad memory location is found. If bad memory is found it will report it otherwise, if the memory stops and no bad cells are found, it will just say "all ram OK".  The other thing Ken did to the original "Blue Ram Utility" is to eliminate the modem codes and almost all of the BASIC; he just left enough to start the program.

After trying the different versions of MESS with the "280 ZZzap/Dodgem" ROM, I see now that the cartridge stopped working correctly with MESS0124 (March 24, 2008).  There seem to have only been two changes to the Astrocade emulator for this version of MESS.  They are:

- [ASTROCDE] Added controls for player 3 and 4 and improved analog controls. [ranger_lennier]
- [ASTROCDE] Removed the MESS specific implementation of the video hardware in favor of the more accurate MAME version. Also fixed the I/O ports defintion which improves the sound a lot. [Dirk Best]

It is probably Dirk's implementation of the MAME video version that causes "Dodgem" to stop working.  I don't need to look into what went wrong, because on September 24, 2013, Richard Degler sent Paul, Lance and myself a detailed email about his testing of MESS 0.150.  He had discovered where MESS was going wrong.  I'd like to post that information-- but I'm still not sure of the correct place to do that.

I think that Lance has mentioned another cartridge that stopped working correctly too.  I can't find it when searching the Bally Alley Yahoo group.  Lance, do you recall which one it was?

13557:
I added an AstroBASIC program from 1984 called "Cubic Rub"by Dorothy Neff.  This program was published in ARCADIAN 6, no. 4 (Feb. 23, 1984): 36.  This program was found in Bob Fabris collection and has not been archived on the BallyAlley website before now.  The program includes a text title screen.

As the program's name suggests, this was inspired by the Rubic's Cube.

You can download the game here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#CubicRub

Instructions from the "Arcadian:"

[The flattened cube is meant to be seen using a mono-spaced font].

    GGG
    GGG
    GGG

WWW RRR YYY OOO
WWW RRR YYY OOO
WWW RRR YYY OOO

    BBB
    BBB
    BBB

CUBIC RUB Instructions:

To play, select cube face by rotating knob - center of cube flashes.

Use joystick right to rotate selected face clockwise.

Use joystick left to rotate selected face counter-clockwise. Use trigger to reset all faces solid.

To load: Enter program, then (first time only) press WORDS GOTO 290 GO. The computer will display the array addresses < *( ) > and you enter the following list of numbers. Now you can save the program by recording it. Play the game with the usual WORDS GO input.


Lately I've been adding unusual programs (mostly applications and utilities) that require extra RAM.  It's nice to add a game that any Astrocade user (with AstroBASIC) can use.

Have fun!

Adam

13562:
I added 1982's AstroBASIC game, "Exterminator," by Phil Bauer to BallyAlley.com.  This is a previously unpublished Arcadian submission.  It includes text title screen.

As with the last program I uploaded ("Cubic Run") this game hasn't been available to use before.

In the Bob Fabris collection was a hand-written letter, game instructions, and hand-written BASIC listing for "Exterminator."  Without them, we'd know nothing about this program at all.  I have also added a BASIC LISTing of the program to the pdf, probably made by Bob Fabris.  You can view it here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#ExterminatorLetter

You can download "Exterminator" here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#ExterminatorBauer

I have typed the letter and instructions to give the game some character so that it is not just an anonymous program floating around the Bally Arcade program area.  The letter has had some basic proofreading done, but I tried to leave it as-is.


June 2, 1982

Mr. Fabris-

The enclosed program on tape in Bally BASIC was created by myself strictly on the information and knowledge of the computer which I learned through the "BASIC" manual and my copies of the "Arcadian."  Since buying my Bally in December 1981, I have been compiling a tape of games and graphics, 75% of which were copied from the BASIC Manual and "Arcadian," the rest are my own.  These (my own) include a Missile Command, Space Destroyers type, Mastermind, and quite a few others I am still experimenting with.

In reading the Arcadian over the months, I have noticed a game called "Exterminator" being sold by a software company.  However, I have never purchased or even seen any of the software advertised in the Arcadian, so I don't know if their "Exterminator" is anything like mine.  I chose the name before I realized it had been used because the asterisks remind me of bugs, etc.  If you deem it necessary and if you use my game, feel free to change its title.  Hopefully the whole idea is different.

Thank you,
Philip Brown


Instructions

Exterminator is a fast-moving maze-type game for up to four players using joystick controls.  Choose no. of players with knob #1.

The game begins with "the exterminator" (player 1) at the heading at the top of the screen.  To reach his pesticides he must make it to the bottom of the screen without being stung (landing on any of the bugs along the way).  Each sweep from the top to bottom or vice versa is limited to the number printed to the right of the heading which will count-down along the way.  Upon reaching the bottom, face color will change green and he now has the pesticide and the power to "exterminate" as many bugs as he can on the way to the top in the allotted number of moves.  Once to the top, color will change to a warning red and he can "go for it again."  Points are scored for each bug exterminated along the way up, the value increasing for the number of times he's made it to the bottom without being "stung."  Some difficulty increases with score.  The higher the score, the more often the "bugs" will appear.  However, the higher the score, the higher the bonus for making it safely back to the top.  If the top is not reached in the allotted time, all points that "sweep" are lost.  Also, a higher score will give a higher count-down number plus extra chances for that player's turn (as indicated by the number next to the right arrow between the player and score).  Over 15,000 points in a turn will give that player an extra turn.  Number of turns for all players is left of heading.  Pull trigger for next player.


Nowadays, I love taking some extra time to archive previously unknown programs like this.  Without some context and instructions, the game is just a name on a list on BallyAlley.

Have fun!

Adam

Added Kevin O'Neill's 1983 AstroBASIC game, "Flaps Up!"  This program was found in the Bob Fabris Collection; it includes a graphic title screen.  This is the games first appearance on BallyAlly.com.  It was published in both:

ARCADIAN 6, no. 2 (Dec. 22, 1983): 11, 13.
Niagara BUG. Bulletin 2, no 4 (1984): 18.

Game Instructions from "Arcadian:"

In this one-player game of skill, you become the pilot of a WWI biplane. After returning from a dangerous mission, you try to land at your home airstrip, only to find that it is being repaired. You receive points for the amount of time you manage to spend on the runway, but watch out! When you see a box of repair supplies ahead, pull up quick or you will collide with it and have 30 points taken from your score. Once you pass 20 boxes, the game will end. A squeeze of the trigger will show you the high score of the day. More squeezes will bring simple instructions, & the game. Have fun with this one!


Enjoy!

13569:
I added Jim Dunson's AstroBASIC art program, "Graphics Quadruplicate." This is an unpublished submission for the $100 "Arcadian" program cash prize.  This program is from the Bob Fabris Collection; it includes a text title screen.

This program uses right angle lines and XY operator to create unusual and very fast graphic art. The program was created to run in AB. It will run in BB, however the effect of speed of operation is lost. The redundancy of LINE statements is deliberate in order to increase the speed of operation.  Four colors are shown in parts 1 & 3 and 8 in part 2.

The program is available here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#GraphicsQuadruplicate

While I was looking for information about this program, I found the original submission letter and BASIC LISTing (with the above program description) that Jim sent to the "Arcadian."  I made them into one pdf and placed them here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#GraphicsQuadruplicate

I also added pictures of the tape (front and back):

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/cassette_pics/misc/misc.html#GraphicsQuad-OpCode

The back of the tape holds another Dunson's program called "64K Data & Opcode Converter," which has previously been archived.

It's great to be able to bring all of these different pieces of this submission back together into one place.  Re-discovering it all is kind of like solving a puzzle.

Have fun!

Adam
13570:
Added the brief instructions for Jim Dunson's "64K Data & Opcode Converter."  I found these brief instructions while searching for background information on the recently uploaded "Graphics Quadruplicate." The following information for the "Converter" program was in the submission letter for Dunson's "Graphics Quadruplicate:"

Experimentation with converting decimal to hex led me to discover that there were no published programs that dealt with the negative decimal. The only one that I could find went from 0 to 32767 or 7FFF. I then developed a very fast entry and easy to use program that converts all 64K.

Decimal      0 to 32767,-32768 to -1

Hexadecimal  0 to FFFF

Binary       0 to 1111 1111 1111 1111

This information has been added to the "64K Data & Opcode Converter" archive, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#64KDataOpCodeConverter

It's always nice to have docs, right?

Enjoy!

Adam

13582:
I think Greg hit the nail on the head... with "well-loved" but working units on eBay going for astronomical prices, it's hard to gauge whether an offer will even be in the ballpark of what someone offering a new system will be looking for.  If I were in the seller's position and someone came at me with a $200 offer, I may well be offended depending on what my preconceived notions were about what it was worth.  From the buyer's perspective, though, those eBay prices seem crazy and only someone with more dollars than sense would pay them.  ;) 

 Also flipping the eBay Best Offer system around to the seller's point of view, I've had things listed for, say, $80 that normally go for $100+ but don't sell very often.  And I would get offers of $40, sometimes even $20.  Even then I don't just shut them down, and I send back a reasonable counter-offer, often trying to meet them close to the middle.  Typically they outright decline without any message or willingness to budge.  The sellers don't know how to sell and the buyers don't know how to buy.
 

 I could only offer $200 myself for even a new Astrocade at this point.  But just as no offense is intended, no offense will be taken if that's not good enough!
13583:
Some people have trouble connecting RF modulators to modern TVs as these lack the matching connectors. I helped many people to connect VCRs and such to televisions because there are many people who just don't understand how the connections work, so, sometimes we can believe the system wasn't tested. I just got an untested Silicon Graphics Indy knowing people would really have trouble finding a 13W3 to VGA adapter - and in case it had minor problems, such as faulty RAM or HD, I would be able to fix it.

First, this is an educational game.  But, for something educational, it sure sounds neat!  So...

I have added the AstroBASIC educational game "Gravity" by Fred Rodney.  This was published in ARCADIAN 6, no. 5 (Mar. 30, 1984): 41, 42.  This Arcadian program was found in the Bob Fabris Collection; it includes a text title screen.

The "Gravity" AstroBASIC program is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/fred_rodney/fred_rodney.html#Gravity

Pictures of the tape for "Gravity" are here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/cassette_pics/fred_rodney/fred_rodney.html#Gravity

The original submission letter, BASIC LISTing and instructions are here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#GravityListing

This program sounds neat to me-- and is based on a C64 program.  It's hard to believe that the Astrocade was still chugging along beside that machine!  Here are the complete instructions which I've OCRed, re-typed (when the original typewriter used cursive script-- ack!) and proofread (to some extent).

From the submission letter to the "Arcadian:"


Dear Robert Fabris,

"The enclosed tape, inspired by the Commodore 64's "Visible Solar System," is an AstroBASIC program that you may wish to publish in the 'Arcadian.'"

I hope that it can supply future programs that will deal with other aspects of space and physical laws.  I hope others will submit programs too, to make a kind of "Arcadian" series of educational programs.

Fred Rodney

P.S.  The "Gravity" program enclosed was written by me and is, to the best of my recollection, an original program that does not intentionally use unauthorized material from other sources.  The program is for the enjoyment and use of "Arcadian" readers.


Fred also included extensive instructions in his original BASIC LISTing.  They are longer, elaborate, and detailed when compared to the instructions originally included in the "Arcadian" when the program was printed.  Here are Fred's original instructions:


*Gravity* by Fred Rodney

You command the first fleet of interplanetary space probes.  You launch them from aboard your command post on the space shuttle Enterprise.  All probes are capable of hovering over any planet at 2000 feet (except Pluto) and each can escape back into space to perform gravitational tests elsewhere.  The probes, however, cannot escape from the gravity and heat of the sun.  All probes that enter the solar atmosphere for tests will disintegrate, but not before sending you the data you seek.  You are left, upon disintegration, with a scene of the night sky from a telescope on your space shuttle.  Since you have an unlimited supply of space probes, the disintegration of a few should not concern you.  Begin with a probe on Earth, for reference.

INSTRUCTIONS: Load the program and the *() array. There is one byte of RAM left on both sides of the array (buffer) so be careful. Run the program. First, you should see the night sky followed by the program title, a little music, and the exhaust from the launch of your shuttle craft. Then a map of the solar system will appear as a reference, with the massive sun on your left. Finally, a menu will appear. Choose a planet to probe from this list by entering the proper number on your keypad (Pluto is not listed because its gravity is not known). After you enter your choice, the map will reappear, highlighting your choice (showing its relative position in the solar system). The screen will then shift to a scene of the planet's surface, with your probe positioned at 2000 feet above the surface. The name of the planet will be on top with its relative gravitational constant (Earth=1) and a seconds clock on the left. After signaling, the probe will release a weight and the clock will time the weight's moment of impact based on the formula: H=1/2gt^2 or t=sqrt(H+1/2g). The menu will reappear and further tests on other planets may be made.

Because of the Astrocade's limited memory, you can only test for gravity with this program. Therefore, this program is called a chapter in a proposed series of educational programs that were inspired by the Commodore 64's "Visible Solar System" cartridge. Future programs will visually compare other features of the solar system and perhaps a venture to another star. Arcadian readers are encouraged to submit "chapters" to this Astrocade Educational "Library." All programs should be factual and fun, and in this context, this program includes a few graphic surprises, using nothing more complicated than an &(9) port setting.

One final note: Don't attempt to set your watch by this program's clock. The final time readings are correct and can easily be checked with a calculator. And this is what really matters. Limited memory precludes the use of the Astrocade's RM variable, I simply felt that the added "frills" were more important because an educational program must be interesting to be used, especially by children. Leave exact seconds (rate of seconds to be precise) to the Analog Clock by George Moses. In addition to the above, the relative gravity constants have a range of 175 with the sun included, but is only *17 without the sun. Most of the activity takes place within this small range, but with the sun included, a difference must be demonstrated within the range of *17 without having to go overboard to demonstrate the tremendous gravity of the sun,

*The column of pixels in the center of the map represents the asteroid belt.


Fred's "Gravity" sure seems to push the edges of the Astrocade; I hope it "attracts" some attention.  When published in the "Arcadian," Mr. Fabris said that if enough follow-up programs were written like this, then maybe they could eventually be put on a cart.  I don't recall any follow-up programs at all, let alone a cart!  I suppose if this had been published earlier, then maybe there would have been a whole series like Fred had originally hoped.

Have fun learning!

Adam

I added a prototype of Ken Lill's "Frustration Fortress" called "Laser Fortress."  This program was found in Ken Lill's tape collection on tape
hand-labeled simply "Games".  This game was eventually printed in the
"Arcadian" as "Frustration Fortress), but here, the title screen calls
it "Laser Fortress, Gambits Tape #1."

This is a one player game.  The object is to get all of the keys in each
 room
without getting hit by any of the randomly firing Laser Cannons.  To
move, use
the joystick (the trigger and knob have no effect).  To get a key, all
you have to do is touch it with the Blinking Box (your piece).

This program is part of the "Frustration Fortress" archive, which was published in ARCADIAN 6, no. 8 (Jun. 30, 1984): 72.  You can download the archive here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_a-h/programs_a-h.html#FrustrationFortress

Ken, you really saved these programs as you want along, didn't you!  It is always a good idea to do that!

Enjoy!

Adam

Here are the complete instructions which I've OCRed, re-typed (when the original typewriter used cursive script-- ack!) and proofread (to some extent).From the submission letter to the "Arcadian:"Dear Robert Fabris,"The enclosed tape, inspired by the Commodore 64's "Visible Solar System," is an AstroBASIC program that you may wish to publish in the 'Arcadian.'"I hope that it can supply future programs that will deal with other aspects of space and physical laws. The program is for the enjoyment and use of "Arcadian" readers.Fred also included extensive instructions in his original BASIC LISTing.  They are longer, elaborate, and detailed when compared to the instructions originally included in the "Arcadian" when the program was printed.  Here are Fred's original instructions:*Gravity* by Fred RodneyYou command the first fleet of interplanetary space probes.  You launch them from aboard your command post on the space shuttle Enterprise.  All probes are capable of hovering over any planet at 2000 feet (except Pluto) and each can escape back into space to perform gravitational tests elsewhere.  The probes, however, cannot escape from the gravity and heat of the sun.  All probes that enter the solar atmosphere for tests will disintegrate, but not before sending you the data you seek.  You are left, upon disintegration, with a scene of the night sky from a telescope on your space shuttle.  Since you have an unlimited supply of space probes, the disintegration of a few should not concern you.  Begin with a probe on Earth, for reference.INSTRUCTIONS: Load the program and the *() array. There is one byte of RAM left on both sides of the array (buffer) so be careful. Run the program. First, you should see the night sky followed by the program title, a little music, and the exhaust from the launch of your shuttle craft. Then a map of the solar system will appear as a reference, with the massive sun on your left. Finally, a menu will appear. Choose a planet to probe from this list by entering the proper number on your keypad (Pluto is not listed because its gravity is not known). After you enter your choice, the map will reappear, highlighting your choice (showing its relative position in the solar system). The screen will then shift to a scene of the planet's surface, with your probe positioned at 2000 feet above the surface. The name of the planet will be on top with its relative gravitational constant (Earth=1) and a seconds clock on the left. After signaling, the probe will release a weight and the clock will time the weight's moment of impact based on the formula: H=1/2gt^2 or t=sqrt(H+1/2g). The menu will reappear and further tests on other planets may be made.Because of the Astrocade's limited memory, you can only test for gravity with this program. Therefore, this program is called a chapter in a proposed series of educational programs that were inspired by the Commodore 64's "Visible Solar System" cartridge. Future programs will visually compare other features of the solar system and perhaps a venture to another star. Arcadian readers are encouraged to submit "chapters" to this Astrocade Educational "Library." All programs should be factual and fun, and in this context, this program includes a few graphic surprises, using nothing more complicated than an &(9) port setting.One final note: Don't attempt to set your watch by this program's clock. The final time readings are correct and can easily be checked with a calculator. And this is what really matters. Limited memory precludes the use of the Astrocade's RM variable, I simply felt that the added "frills" were more important because an educational program must be interesting to be used, especially by children. Leave exact seconds (rate of seconds to be precise) to the Analog Clock by George Moses. In addition to the above, the relative gravity constants have a range of 175 with the sun included, but is only *17 without the sun. Most of the activity takes place within this small range, but with the sun included, a difference must be demonstrated within the range of *17 without having to go overboard to demonstrate the tremendous gravity of the sun,*The column of pixels in the center of the map represents the asteroid belt.Fred's "Gravity" sure seems to push the edges of the Astrocade; I hope it "attracts" some attention.  When published in the "Arcadian," Mr. Fabris said that if enough follow-up programs were written like this, then maybe they could eventually be put on a cart.  I don't recall any follow-up programs at all, let alone a cart!  I suppose if this had been published earlier, then maybe there would have been a whole series like Fred had originally hoped.Have fun learning!Adam

I added 1984's AstroBASIC program, "Morse Code Practice," by John Hedstrom to BallyAlley.com.  This program was found in the Bob Fabris Collection.  It was printed in:

ARCADIAN 6, no. 8 (Jun. 30, 1984): 70. (Original program listing and docs)
ARCADIAN 6, no. 8 (Jun. 30, 1984): 79. (Additions: Notes and Fixes)

You can download the program here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_i-p/programs_i-p.html#MorseCodePractice

These instructions are combined from the original printing of the program and the follow-up issue with bug fixes and additional information:


"Morse Code Practice" will enable you to brush-up on your code.  The timing has been adjusted to accepted standards.  You can select between given categories including a "custom" selection.

Speeds 1-9 correspond to 36, 24, 18, 14, 12, 10, 9, 8, and 7 words per minute.  In the Custom mode, 9 characters are needed to make an entry.  If your item as only six characters, then add three spaces to fill out the required 9.  The punctuation selection requires 10 array values to be added [these are listed in "Arcadian" along with array entry program].


There are several Morse code programs for the Astrocade.  It seems to have been a popular subject.  As a cub scout in elementary school, I remember that this was something we talked about-- it may also have been in the Cub Scout book (I can't remember for sure).  I looked up Morse Code Trainer, and what do you know, there is an online one at "Boy's Life" (the Boy Scout magazine):

http://boyslife.org/games/online-games/575/morse-code-machine/

I guess they have an Astrocade hooked up to the internet as a server.  Or should, right?

Enjoy!

Adam

I have added the AstroBASIC educational game "Gravity" by Fred Rodney.  This was published in ARCADIAN 6, no. 5 (Mar. 30, 1984): 41, 42.  This Arcadian program was found in the Bob Fabris Collection; it includes a text title screen.

This program sounds neat to me-- and is based on a C64 program.  It's hard to believe that the Astrocade was still chugging along beside that machine!  Here are the complete instructions which I've OCRed, re-typed (when the original typewriter used cursive script-- ack!) and proofread (to some extent).

From the submission letter to the "Arcadian:"


Dear Robert Fabris,

"The enclosed tape, inspired by the Commodore 64's "Visible Solar System," is an AstroBASIC program that you may wish to publish in the 'Arcadian.'"

I hope that it can supply future programs that will deal with other aspects of space and physical laws.  I hope others will submit programs too, to make a kind of "Arcadian" series of educational programs.

Fred Rodney

P.S.  The "Gravity" program enclosed was written by me and is, to the best of my recollection, an original program that does not intentionally use unauthorized material from other sources.  The program is for the enjoyment and use of "Arcadian" readers.


Fred also included extensive instructions in his original BASIC LISTing.  They are longer, elaborate, and detailed when compared to the instructions originally included in the "Arcadian" when the program was printed.  Here are Fred's original instructions:


*Gravity* by Fred Rodney

You command the first fleet of interplanetary space probes.  You launch them from aboard your command post on the space shuttle Enterprise.  All probes are capable of hovering over any planet at 2000 feet (except Pluto) and each can escape back into space to perform gravitational tests elsewhere.  The probes, however, cannot escape from the gravity and heat of the sun.  All probes that enter the solar atmosphere for tests will disintegrate, but not before sending you the data you seek.  You are left, upon disintegration, with a scene of the night sky from a telescope on your space shuttle.  Since you have an unlimited supply of space probes, the disintegration of a few should not concern you.  Begin with a probe on Earth, for reference.

INSTRUCTIONS: Load the program and the *() array. There is one byte of RAM left on both sides of the array (buffer) so be careful. Run the program. First, you should see the night sky followed by the program title, a little music, and the exhaust from the launch of your shuttle craft. Then a map of the solar system will appear as a reference, with the massive sun on your left. Finally, a menu will appear. Choose a planet to probe from this list by entering the proper number on your keypad (Pluto is not listed because its gravity is not known). After you enter your choice, the map will reappear, highlighting your choice (showing its relative position in the solar system). The screen will then shift to a scene of the planet's surface, with your probe positioned at 2000 feet above the surface. The name of the planet will be on top with its relative gravitational constant (Earth=1) and a seconds clock on the left. After signaling, the probe will release a weight and the clock will time the weight's moment of impact based on the formula: H=1/2gt^2 or t=sqrt(H+1/2g). The menu will reappear and further tests on other planets may be made.

Because of the Astrocade's limited memory, you can only test for gravity with this program. Therefore, this program is called a chapter in a proposed series of educational programs that were inspired by the Commodore 64's "Visible Solar System" cartridge. Future programs will visually compare other features of the solar system and perhaps a venture to another star. Arcadian readers are encouraged to submit "chapters" to this Astrocade Educational "Library." All programs should be factual and fun, and in this context, this program includes a few graphic surprises, using nothing more complicated than an &(9) port setting.

One final note: Don't attempt to set your watch by this program's clock. The final time readings are correct and can easily be checked with a calculator. And this is what really matters. Limited memory precludes the use of the Astrocade's RM variable, I simply felt that the added "frills" were more important because an educational program must be interesting to be used, especially by children. Leave exact seconds (rate of seconds to be precise) to the Analog Clock by George Moses. In addition to the above, the relative gravity constants have a range of 175 with the sun included, but is only *17 without the sun. Most of the activity takes place within this small range, but with the sun included, a difference must be demonstrated within the range of *17 without having to go overboard to demonstrate the tremendous gravity of the sun,

*The column of pixels in the center of the map represents the asteroid belt.


Fred's "Gravity" sure seems to push the edges of the Astrocade; I hope it "attracts" some attention.  When published in the "Arcadian," Mr. Fabris said that if enough follow-up programs were written like this, then maybe they could eventually be put on a cart.  I don't recall any follow-up programs at all, let alone a cart!  I suppose if this had been published earlier, then maybe there would have been a whole series like Fred had originally hoped.

Have fun learning!

Adam

    First, this is an educational game.  But, for something educational, it sure sounds neat!  So...

I have added the AstroBASIC educational game "Gravity" by Fred Rodney.  This was published in ARCADIAN 6, no. 5 (Mar. 30, 1984): 41, 42.  This Arcadian program was found in the Bob Fabris Collection; it includes a text title screen.

The "Gravity" AstroBASIC program is here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/fred_rodney/fred_rodney.html#Gravity

Pictures of the tape for "Gravity" are here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/cassette_pics/fred_rodney/fred_rodney.html#Gravity

The original submission letter, BASIC LISTing and instructions are here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#GravityListing

This program sounds neat to me-- and is based on a C64 program.  It's hard to believe that the Astrocade was still chugging along beside that machine!  Here are the complete instructions which I've OCRed, re-typed (when the original typewriter used cursive script-- ack!) and proofread (to some extent).

From the submission letter to the "Arcadian:"


Dear Robert Fabris,

"The enclosed tape, inspired by the Commodore 64's "Visible Solar System," is an AstroBASIC program that you may wish to publish in the 'Arcadian.'"

I hope that it can supply future programs that will deal with other aspects of space and physical laws.  I hope others will submit programs too, to make a kind of "Arcadian" series of educational programs.

Fred Rodney

P.S.  The "Gravity" program enclosed was written by me and is, to the best of my recollection, an original program that does not intentionally use unauthorized material from other sources.  The program is for the enjoyment and use of "Arcadian" readers.


Fred also included extensive instructions in his original BASIC LISTing.  They are longer, elaborate, and detailed when compared to the instructions originally included in the "Arcadian" when the program was printed.  Here are Fred's original instructions:


*Gravity* by Fred Rodney

You command the first fleet of interplanetary space probes.  You launch them from aboard your command post on the space shuttle Enterprise.  All probes are capable of hovering over any planet at 2000 feet (except Pluto) and each can escape back into space to perform gravitational tests elsewhere.  The probes, however, cannot escape from the gravity and heat of the sun.  All probes that enter the solar atmosphere for tests will disintegrate, but not before sending you the data you seek.  You are left, upon disintegration, with a scene of the night sky from a telescope on your space shuttle.  Since you have an unlimited supply of space probes, the disintegration of a few should not concern you.  Begin with a probe on Earth, for reference.

INSTRUCTIONS: Load the program and the *() array. There is one byte of RAM left on both sides of the array (buffer) so be careful. Run the program. First, you should see the night sky followed by the program title, a little music, and the exhaust from the launch of your shuttle craft. Then a map of the solar system will appear as a reference, with the massive sun on your left. Finally, a menu will appear. Choose a planet to probe from this list by entering the proper number on your keypad (Pluto is not listed because its gravity is not known). After you enter your choice, the map will reappear, highlighting your choice (showing its relative position in the solar system). The screen will then shift to a scene of the planet's surface, with your probe positioned at 2000 feet above the surface. The name of the planet will be on top with its relative gravitational constant (Earth=1) and a seconds clock on the left. After signaling, the probe will release a weight and the clock will time the weight's moment of impact based on the formula: H=1/2gt^2 or t=sqrt(H+1/2g). The menu will reappear and further tests on other planets may be made.

Because of the Astrocade's limited memory, you can only test for gravity with this program. Therefore, this program is called a chapter in a proposed series of educational programs that were inspired by the Commodore 64's "Visible Solar System" cartridge. Future programs will visually compare other features of the solar system and perhaps a venture to another star. Arcadian readers are encouraged to submit "chapters" to this Astrocade Educational "Library." All programs should be factual and fun, and in this context, this program includes a few graphic surprises, using nothing more complicated than an &(9) port setting.

One final note: Don't attempt to set your watch by this program's clock. The final time readings are correct and can easily be checked with a calculator. And this is what really matters. Limited memory precludes the use of the Astrocade's RM variable, I simply felt that the added "frills" were more important because an educational program must be interesting to be used, especially by children. Leave exact seconds (rate of seconds to be precise) to the Analog Clock by George Moses. In addition to the above, the relative gravity constants have a range of 175 with the sun included, but is only *17 without the sun. Most of the activity takes place within this small range, but with the sun included, a difference must be demonstrated within the range of *17 without having to go overboard to demonstrate the tremendous gravity of the sun,

*The column of pixels in the center of the map represents the asteroid belt.


Fred's "Gravity" sure seems to push the edges of the Astrocade; I hope it "attracts" some attention.  When published in the "Arcadian," Mr. Fabris said that if enough follow-up programs were written like this, then maybe they could eventually be put on a cart.  I don't recall any follow-up programs at all, let alone a cart!  I suppose if this had been published earlier, then maybe there would have been a whole series like Fred had originally hoped.

Have fun learning!

Adam

I added 1984's "Round Robin Utility" by John Hammond.  This AstroBASIC program was published in ARCADIAN 6, no. 6 (Apr. 20, 1984): 56.  This "Arcadian" program was found in Bob Fabris collection; it includes a graphic title screen.

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_q-z/programs_q-z.html#RoundRobinUtility

Instructions from the "Arcadian:"

This program generates the opponent pairings in a round robin competition for three to 999 teams. The program begins with a set-up menu:

1.  Enter the number of teams (3-999)

2.  Enter the starting round to be displayed (enter 1 when all rounds are required).

3.  Enter the team numbers to be displayed (enter 0 when all teams are required).

A maximum of 16 opponent pairings will be displayed on one screen. When more pairings are required for a round or when the display for a round is complete the program computes the next screen's information; and when ready, a down arrow is displayed. Enter LIST or 'divide' sign to end the display and RETURN to set up menu. Enter NEXT or 'multiply' to bypass the remainder of the round presently being displayed. Press any other key to display the next screen. When a round is complete, the program returns to the setup menu.


This is a pretty unusual program with very specific needs.  Has/does anyone here use round robin scheduling?  If so, then what do you use it for?

Have fun all you, uh, round robin users...!

I added another version of 1983's "Locksmith" by Don Crider.  This version has a title screen.  The version was was previously online is still available, but it is now considered an alternate version.  This BASIC games was published in ARCADIAN 5, no. 10 (Aug. 16, 1983): 157.

This game is the August 1983 $100 prize winner for the month.  Unlike most programs released in 1983 (and later), "Locksmith" is compatible with both versions of Bally and Astro BASIC.  The instructions in the Arcadian are extremely terse and consist of an extremely small line-drawing of the screen with the text:

Object - Line-up slots with arrow at top.
JX moves slots.
JY selects line.

These are the exact same instructions that Mr. Crider included with his undated program submission letter to the "Arcadian."

For those who have never seen the game at all, the slightly-helpful graphic is available here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_5/arcadian_vol_5_issue_10.pdf#Page=9

This program was found in the Bob Fabris Collection; it includes a graphic title screen.  An alternate version is also included in the archive, which does not have the title screen.  As far as Paul knows, it's the same program.  Sometimes, people would include these title screens when submitting programs to the Arcadian, even though they couldn't be reproduced when the program was printed.

I haven't played this program myself (that I can remember).  Does anyone recall playing this game?

If you haven't tried it, then give it a whirl and report back to us.  You know you wanna play it, because you're curious and you wanna...

have fun!

I added an AstroBASIC program called "Letter Writer" by George Moses.  This program is from the early or mid-1980s.  This program prints a letter from George Moses to Ken Lill to the screen.  You can download it here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/george_moses/misc_progs/misc_progs.html#LetterWriter

If anyone re-types this letter from the screen, then I'll add it to the BallyAlley website.

"Letter Writer" was found in Ken Lill's tape collection.  The garbage on the screen, when the program is loading, is correct.  A Blue RAM BASIC version was on the same tape.  As far as Paul knows, this program is not related to "Letter Writer" by Clyde Perkins.

Paul doesn't see anything that would print to an actual printer; it just prints a letter to the screen. The letter isn't in the code itself, so George must have saved it in the screen memory, which is why you see a bunch of seemingly random garbage when you load the program.  This certainly wasn't easier than just writing a letter down, but it's interesting what people were able to make the Astrocade do with their so-called game console.

Have fun!

13605:
Added 1983's "Swordfight" by Brian Hildebrand.  This BASIC game "germ" of a game was published in ARCADIAN 5, no. 5 (Mar. 14, 1983): 80.  This game was found in the Bob Fabris Collection; it includes a text title screen.

You can download the program here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/arcadian/programs_q-z/programs_q-z.html#Swordfight

Instructions from the "Arcadian:"

Swordfight is a first program by Brian, and is included herein to give the game makers the germ for a new game.  This would actually be a subroutine where one needed a swinging arm (sword) and readout if a touch was made.  Other routines would put a body around the arm, move the complete body around, add background, etc.  Let us know if you come up with something!

Use the joystick to position the 'base' and the knob to rotate the sword. The computer will automatically tell you if you've made the touch, while the trigger will start over.

For BB users, there's an opportunity in Line 220 for you to apply the lessons given by George Moses on page 58.


The George Moses "lessons" that are referred to in the above directions are located in ARCADIAN 5, no. 4 (Feb. 18, 1983): 58-59.   George discusses how to convert AstroBASIC sound variables to Bally BASIC sound ports.  Line 220 uses the AstroBASIC's new sound variables (not available in Bally BASIC).  To make the sound effects work properly requires a user to convert these effects for the older Bally BASIC.

Here is a direct link to those directions:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_5/arcadian_vol_5_issue_04.pdf#Page=4


Brian own statements about this program (from his submission letter and program LISTing) are quite different from Bob.

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/letters/letters.html#Swordfight


Brian says:

Swordfight is a simple game. Controller #1 operates the left man and controller #2 operates the right man. The object is to place the tip of your sword on your opponent "TOUCHE".

The controls are easy, the joystick operates your position and the knob swings the sword. The sword only goes 180 degrees so it serves no purpose to get behind your opponent, besides you wouldn't stab him in the back, would you?

If the score gets too ridiculous just pull trigger #1, the last scores will show and then all variables are reset.

This program could use improvement and I'm open for suggestions, I would like to learn a lot more about programing.


Brian's submission letter (which I'm 99% sure accompanies "Swordfight," and not one of his other submitted program) is quite neat, and is also worth a read to see how people view the Astrocade community and the goings-on of the game industry at the time.  I wonder how old Brian was when he wrote and submitted this game?  He seems young.

Enjoy!

Adam
13606:
Bug Fix for Bill Mead's "Battleship"

In a 1982 letter in the Bob Fabris Collection from Joe Peoples to Bob Farbis, Joe points out a bug, and provides a fix, for Bill Mead's "Battleship" for Bally BASIC (not the AstroBASIC reprint).  This was published in: ARCADIAN 4, no. 9 (Jul. 06, 1982): 93.  The line, as originally printed, read:

40 IF V>32V=2

That line should be:

40 IF V>32V=32

I know that this fix is correct, as the AstroBASIC reprint of "Battleship" includes this fix.  However, I don't think that the bug fix was ever printed.  Now, 33 yeas later, it's been noted.  Thanks, Joe... wherever you are!

13610:
I the AstroBASIC version of "Treasure Hunt" by Scott Walpole.  It can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/misc.html#TreasureHuntWalpole


This is an unpublished "Arcadian" game submission found in the Bob Fabris collection.  It was submitted on May 25, 1983 to the newsletter for consideration for the $100 monthly programming contest.

The complete instructions for this game are available online.  A portion of the directions are included here, but the detailed table with the objects, their descriptions, their point value and the number of occurrences of each object is omitted from this excerpt:


"Treasure Hunt" is played on a 9x15 grid. Hidden under the squares in the grid are objects randomly placed by the computer at the beginning of the game. Each player, in turn, selects one square by moving the marker with the joystick and uncovers it by pulling the trigger of his hand control. The object of the game is to first find four hidden "keys" represented by the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4. After finding the keys, the treasure will be "unlocked", and the player who finds it will score 500 points.

Enter the number of players (from 1 to 4) at the beginning of the game when the "P" appears in the upper left corner of the screen. Player 1 begins by uncovering a square. Under each square is an object that may help or hinder your search for the keys. These objects are described in the table below. The four keys must be found in numerical order, from 1 to 4, before you can get the treasure.

The winner is the player who has the highest score at the end of the game. The game ends when the treasure is found.

Other Features:

Moving Objects: All objects move to a new square after being found, leaving the previously occupied square blank. The only exceptions are the keys, the treasure, and the lose-a-turn symbol which remain in one place throughout the game.

Double Score: When "2X SCORE" appears, all point values will be doubled for the next round. Solitaire: One player can play alone trying to score as few points as possible.


The full instructions, program submission letter and BASIC LISTing can be read downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/basic/basic.html#TreasureHuntLISTing

Enjoy!

Instructions for "Artillery Duel" from "Arcadian:"

"Artillery Duel" is an intriguing game by John Perkins. The machine sets up a random ground and adds two gun emplacements. As each player's turn is taken, he adjusts the knob for barrel elevation, moves the joystick to add or reduce the number of powder bags (by whole bags, sideways; by tenths, back and forth). Then when ready, pull the trigger. There is gravity and a random wind. Anyway, the gun recoils and there goes the shell. There is an explosion when it lands. A gun is destroyed when less than half a gun remains (the repair crew can replace a gun barrel). The program uses all available space- don't enter lines 3 & 4. Be sure to exercise the joystick to see how the variables work.


Reprints and Re-Issues of "Artillery Duel:"

"Artillery Duel" is such an outstanding game that Astrocade, Inc. reprinted it in the "AstroBASIC" manual (this is the manual that comes with the BASIC cartridge that includes the build-in interface).  Both editions of the AstroBASIC manual's re-printing had errors which were corrected in the "Arcadian newsletter:"

"Bally BASIC Handbook," Pages 95-96.   (Referred to as the AstroBASIC Manual)
ARCADIAN 4, no. 4 (Jan. 22, 1982): 36. (AstroBASIC Manual, 1'st ed. Correction)
ARCADIAN 4, no. 5 (Mar. 05, 1982): 46. ("Best of Arcadian - 1980" Announcement)
ARCADIAN 5, no. 4 (Feb. 18, 1983): 56. (AstroBASIC Manual, 2'nd ed. Correction)
ARCADIAN 5, no. 5 (Mar. 14, 1983): 77. (Correction to page 56 correction)


Instructions for "Artillery Duel" from "AstroBASIC Manual:"

Artillery Duel is an intriguing game submitted courtesy of "The Arcadian," a monthly newsletter serving the Bally BASIC programming hobbyist and published by Bob Fabris. This program sets up a random mountain scene and adds two gun emplacements. As each player's turn is taken, he adjusts the knob for barrel elevation, moves the joystick to add or reduce the number of gunpowder bags (by whole bags sideways; by tenths back and forth). Then when ready, pull the trigger. There is gravity and a random wind. The gun recoils and fires the shell. There is an explosion when it lands. A gun is destroyed when less than half a gun remains (the repair crew can replace a gun barrel). The program uses all available space, so don't enter lines 3 and 4. Be sure to exercise the joystick to see how the variables work.


Have fun!

Both versions of "Artillery Duel," as listed in the AstroBASIC manual, have misprints in them.  The "Arcadian" lists the corrections here:

ARCADIAN 4, no. 4 (Jan. 22, 1982): 36. (AstroBASIC Manual, 1'st ed. Correction)
ARCADIAN 5, no. 4 (Feb. 18, 1983): 56. (AstroBASIC Manual, 2'nd ed. Correction)
ARCADIAN 5, no. 5 (Mar. 14, 1983): 77. (Correction to page 56 correction)

Both the second and first printing of the AstroBASIC manuals have quite a few differences between them.  Richard Degler recorded all of them that he could find here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/BASIC_Manual_Differences.txt

The exact differences (as listed by Richard, above) are:

Pg. 95  - In the listing when they fixed line number 190 to show that you need
          a space (and not a GO) between "IF W" and the following "TV=", they
          erased the '5' in line 170 where it once had "P/5+1" (I used the '/'
          as the divide's sign.)

          One of the saddest mistakes, to me, is that Artillery Duel has a
          mistake in the first edition of the AstroBASIC manual that makes it so
          that it won't work correctly.  The second version of the manual fixes
          that problem but has an entirely different set of mistakes.  The
          Arcadian has the fixes for these.

          ARCADIAN, 4, no. 4 (Jan. 22, 1982): 36.

          ASTRO-BASIC (REV. 1) MANUAL CORRECTION     There is a direct typo in
          the program "Artillery Duel" on page 95.  In line 430, where BC is
          controlled, the printer dropped the initial "R" in the Random command,
          so change the printed portion to read     BC=RND(3)x13+86     Then in
          line 190, when entering this line, be certain to leave a space after
          the IF statement.  The printed line overflow to the next line has
          caused some confusion.  This portion of the line should look like
          this:  IF W TV=95+(W>0)X2

          ARCADIAN, 5, no. 4 (Feb. 18, 1982): 56.

          ARTILLERY DUEL CORRECTIONS required in the newest Basic Manual (that
          comes with the #6004 Basic Videocade).... As an identifier, the older
          version of the Manual has two printings of "Perspectives" on page 90.
          Now that you know which version you have, those with the newer one
          should make two corrections in Artillery Duel on page 95.  Line 170
          should read
               170 P=(S=1)x5;C=P-5+1
          and line 350 should read
               350 BOX 0,36,159,16,2; BOX (P+1),(P+2)+1,3,1,1

I added 1980's "Connect Four" by Robert Leake.  This Bally BASIC game was found in the Ken Lill Collection on a tape.  The program was printed here:

CURSOR 2, no. 1 (August 1980): 51-54. (Original Printing)
ARCADIAN 6, no. 9 (Jul. 27, 1984): 79-88. (Program Reprint)

You can download the game here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/300_baud_programs/cursor/cursor.html#ConnectFourRobertLeake

This game was one of the more difficult BASIC programs to type into Bally BASIC-- and it certainly it was the most hard to read.  To see the original listing and instructions (and an explanation of why it was so hard to enter), read the overview here-- where the newsletter can be downloaded:

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/cursor/cursor.html#CURSORAugust1980

Fred Cornett, the editor of Cursor thought very highly of "Connect Four." In his 1980 editor's note he wrote, "This is the finest board game program we have ever seen written for the 'Bally!' The graphics, color and sound are excellent. The computer makes each move totally cognizant of all the ramifications of his move. Hence, you are forced to play very well indeed in order to win (it beats us 8 out of 10 times). This program alone is well worth the $9.75 subscription price for 'Cursor.' Paul Thacker (when archiving this program in 2013) thought differently, he noted, "The A.I. let me win in four turns."

The object of this game is to get four of your playing pieces in a row (without any of your opponent's pieces in between) vertically, horizontally or diagonally before the computer or your human opponent does.

Pieces drop vertically in the selected column to the lowest unoccupied position. To select a column, move the joystick left or right and squeeze trigger when indicator is over desired column. Joystick 1 always goes first.

The full instructions, in text format, for this game, as printed in the "Cursor" newsletter, are here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/cursor_basic-express/connect%20four/Connect%20Four%20%28Archive%20Info%29%28with%20EOL%29.txt

For those who want to gave this game a try (and wish to load the game with AstroBASIC), then it's nice to know that the 2000-baud version of Robert Leake's "Connect Four" is already on Ballyalley.com, here:
