I found a great video on YouTube posted by MediaBurnArchive.  Most of the video's footage is from around 1982.  The video features LOTS of color video of Ms. Gorf.  and a great, though partial, interview with Jamie Fenton.  If you look in the background, Jamie has an Astrocade on the back shelf pretty-close to the prototype of Ms. Gorf.  Also featured is Eugene Jarvis trying to figure-out how to play "The Adventures of Robby Roto!"

I'd love to hear comments from people about this video and the other Jamie Fenton links (below) if you watch them.

Here is the link on YouTube:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AretGtg4GHQ

Here is a full description for the video:

When a group of independent video makers set out to document current tech trends for an ill-fated television show called Wired In, they hardly suspected they were capturing an industry poised on the edge of cataclysmic change. Like many young tech industries, video games were hot, and everyone wanted to get in on the action, but as more and more companies jumped in, often with subpar products, the bubble just grew and grew. In 1982, when this footage was shot, the North American video game industry was at its peak. One year later, the bubble burst in what is now known as the video game crash of 1983.

It was a major blow to a fledgling industry, and the landscape was forever changed. North America, which had been a major player, took the hardest hit, and Japan took over as the single leading producer of gaming consoles and software for next 30+ years.

Nonetheless, signs off the impending crash were starting to appear back in 1982, and perhaps the most poignant story captured in our archive is that of Jamie (FKA Jay) Fenton, a game designer at Bally-Midway whose game, The Adventures of Robby Roto, would in some ways mimic the industry's own fate.

In the video above, Fenton also shows off Ms. Gorf, a game she was working on at the time that would, ultimately, become a victim of the crash. The game has never been released, even unofficially, and footage of it in action is incredibly rare. She also talks a little bit about the future of video games, and proves to be surprisingly prescient.

Greg Bunting wrote:
>>
[I wondered] if a emulator can be made to run on the Xbox or other home consoles such as that.
>>

I know that you can run emulators on at least on some of the older, but modern-ish, consoles (i.e. original Xbox), but I think the systems always have to be hacked/modded or at the very least use exploits (in the case of the GameCube).  I've seen both the Xbox and Wii run emulators quite well, and I'd be surprised if most of the modern systems can't run them in some way.  However, the best experience for emulation will be on the PCs (Mac and Windows).  The emulators that the consoles run are usually (always?) ports of freely distributable emulators on the PC.

>>
 I like the games but just seem afraid to play the actual system due to
units having a big failure rate.
>>

I know your pain with the Astrocade, as I've had units die on me before.  Then again, I've also had an Intelllivision and and least two Colecovisions die on me while they were being used.  I once had a Commodore monitor catch fire while I was in another room-- that was scary (it was this event that made me REALLY appreciate the fire retardant in the plastic that makes the old systems turn yellow).  I was at a classic game festival and I saw an Intellivision that belonged to someone else die while we were using it.  He told me he'd had several Intellivisions give up the ghost on him.  The difference with these other systems is that they are easily replaceable.  I'm not afraid to run my own Astrocades, but I nearly always do it with the case open and a fan blowing over the voltage regulator and the data chip.  Does that invite static?  Probably a bit.  I've heard a few people who have opened their working Astrocade and taken out the RF shield and then system has died.  I'm really not sure what the safest bet with the Astrocade is while it's in use.  Whatever it is, I know that NOT using it will make it die too.  Of neglect.

Adam

13640:
All I can say is "Wow, do I look young in those photos..." 

 It was a great time for me. I was learning about computers. Learning about assembly code, and graphics. Specifically, how to synchronize the software to the hardware so there would be no flicker when I drew to the screen.
 

 The idea was you wait for the vertical interrupt, because the display hardware is not updating the screen, then draw as much graphics as you can before the display hardware tries to draw the part of memory you are changing.
 

 This simple concept led to do eventually designing video boards, and later computers for Apple. I have a lot to thank that little Bally Arcade for.
 

 And it was a great time for collaboration. I enjoyed talking with all the other guys doing amazing things. One favorite thing was Craig Anderson's "Computer Ear" where he 'listened' to what you were saying and pattern matched the input with stored commands. It was my first 'hands on' experience with voice command.
 

 We were all hopeful that a more powerful "Z-Grass" system would one day be available for consumers. But alas, that was not to be. Although I did work on the DataMax UV-1 development system which ran Z-Grass. But I was not impressed with that system and built my own 'cartridge development environment' using a friends TRS-80 and expansion chassis.
 

 It was a great time of learning, exploring and camaraderie. I was always the guy that built the tools. And folks like George Moses would use those tools to do things like all the music he wrote for the Arcade. This continued in my life with designing video boards and computers.
 

 I was very fortunate to have worked with the Bally Arcade. It had a large influence on my life. Without the Arcade, there would be no Mac Mini, Apple TV, or even iPad (things my team worked on at Apple). Well, maybe someone else would have created those things for Apple. But I like to think my team did a better job on those products than others could have...

Brett Bilbrey, on July 12, 2015, wrote:
>>
All I can say is "Wow, do I look young in those photos..."
>>

Those two Bally Arcade user-group meetings took place about thirty-five years ago.  Brett, I presume that you were around twenty at the time.  If you hadn't have noticeably aged, then I would have been quite surprised!

Yesterday I attended a family reunion (of sorts); people saw me that had not seen me in forty (!) years.  They couldn't believe it has been "that long!"  Two of the people started crying when they talked babysitting me when I was still in my crib.  Brett, was looking at the pictures from the "Arcadian" like that at all?  Is it hard for you to believe that so much time has passed?   Do you feel like you're a different person now, or the same person with much more experience?  Would your 1980-self recognize the person that you are today?

>>
It was a great time for me.
>>

I've noticed that a current thread that runs through most classic-gaming podcasts is that people generally feel that computers were more "fun" in the 70s and 80s.  How do you feel about that?

>>
 I was learning […] how to synchronize the software to the hardware so there would be no flicker when I drew to the screen.
>>

It's each to see that Brett took time his time to create his two cartridge games: "ICBM Attack" and "Treasure Cove"   The two cartridge games look great-- and very colorful too.  The animation in "Treasure Cove" is particularly great.  Brett lent me his collection of Spectre material used to create the games and it gives quite an insight into the development of both games.  You can view that material here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/spectre_systems/spectre_systems.html

>>
One favorite thing was Craig Anderson's "Computer Ear" where he 'listened' to what you were saying and pattern matched the input with stored commands.
>>

There are pictures of the "Computer Ear" here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/Computer_Ear/computer_ear.html

Craig has mentioned on this message board that the software for the "Computer Ear" hardware was written in BASIC, but it just wasn't fast enough to work like he envisioned it.  He wished that it had all been written in machine language.

>>
I did work on the DataMax UV-1 development system which ran Z-Grass. But I was not impressed with that system and built my own 'cartridge development environment' using a friends TRS-80 and expansion chassis.
>>

Brett, you were trying to use the DataMax UV-1 at Nutting Associates to create games for the unexpanded Astrocade.  You had a problem with the system mainly because you were targeting games for the Astrocade, yet you weren't writing the code in assembly language.  The system was aimed, I think, at cable operators and animators.   I presume that it had the ability to act as a genlock right out of the box.  Here are some general questions I have about the Datamax UV-1:

1) If the UV-1 had had a wide release (rather than a limited release of, probably, in the low-hundreds of units), how do you feel that the UV-1 would have been accepted by home users/cable operators who wanted to use the Z-GRASS language to create animations (not necessarily games) targeted for the UV-1 itself?

2) The UV-1 had RAM disks and a real DOS; did it have a blitter chip?

3) Was there any additional hardware that made the UV-1 similar to the high-res games (like "Gorf" or "Wizard of Wor") that were released in the arcade that used the Astrocade chipset?

4) Was there anything that you enjoyed using the UV-1 system for at all?  For instance, were there any small improvement that could have been made to the UV-1 that would have helped you program the 4K Bally Arcade?

>>
Without the [Bally] Arcade, there would be no Mac Mini, Apple TV, or even iPad (things my team worked on at Apple).
>>

No Astrocade = No iPad: a bold statement; I like it!  In context, that quote makes sense.  Out of context it would look very strange.  Okay, Brett, when is Apple going to update the original Bally Arcade and make it portable?!?

Yep, I'm 55 now. You pretty much nailed the dates. 

 Well, I was not crying, but it was a 'flashback'. "Who is that young kid?" ;-)
 

 I've had many 'phases' of my life...
 - Growing up and grade school.
 - High School
 - College
 - My first job at Bally/Dave Nutting Associates (Also Action Graphics, Spectre Systems, etc.) 
 - Working at Fredericksen and Shu Labs (what DNA became after the fall of the video game industry)
 - Working at Intelligent Resources (designing video boards for computers)
 - Working at Intelligent Paradigm (designing broadcast video hardware)
 - Working at Apple (designing computers)
 - And now semi-retired (that is, waiting for something fun to do next...)
 

 So to answer your question, today I am very much a different person than I was back then. But I would hope my 1980-self would be proud of the person I have become.
 

 Yep. Things were indeed 'more fun' back in the day. It is hard to quickly quantify why, but the feeling of discovery, and wild west, made it much more fun back then.
 

 As to the DataMax UV-1...
 

 What I did not like most was the 'Terse Fourth' language they used for programming... 'yuck'  ;-)

 2) I don't know. That would be a question for Jeff Frederiksen. If I ever knew, I have long since forgot...

 Datamax UV-1 - Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Datamax_UV-1 The Datamax UV-1 was a pioneering computer designed by a group of computer graphics artists working at the University of Illinois at Chicago, known ...

 Preview by Yahoo 
 
 
 This wikipedia article speaks to the configuration better than I can remember...
 

 The UV-1 was basically a computer that used Bally's video display. So it 'could' run games and such.

Hello, All -
 

 After getting into retrogaming a decade ago and then kind of putting it on hold, all my systems are gone (well, pre-Xbox systems) - but I jumped back in the pool and have picked up some consoles off of eBay! The star of the show of course, is my Astrocade. It appears to be a first generation retail, as it's not white (i understand the mail order units were white), and the lid I believe has the initial branding (Home Library Computer). 
 

 I haven't tested it yet - turns out the RF adapter I ordered was the wrong one so I just ordered a new one (hope I got the right one - this is what I ordered: http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0002J25OI?psc=1&redirect=true&ref_=oh_aui_detailpage_o00_s00 http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0002J25OI?psc=1&redirect=true&ref_=oh_aui_detailpage_o00_s00) and I think it arrives Monday and I should be able to conduct a test! Oh yes, the Bally was listed as untested, so I took a gamble. I am really just getting acquainted with a lot of the online community and resources in this area; I posted on AtariAge and Adam invited me here - he had responded to my post asking for any advice on using/maintaining the Bally. 
 

 So I wanted to intro myself and ask if any of you have input. I'll post some pics, perhaps tonight. Please keep in mind - I am not very technically savvy. From perusing some posts, I can tell many of you are. So from time to time, I may have to ask you to rephrase something as if you're talking to a child!
 

 I also picked up a Channel F, but it hasn't arrived yet. Thought I'd mention that - unless this forum is really brand-loyal and don't want to discuss other systems! 
 

 So any tips on cleaning/maintaining, anything. For example, Adam and others mentioned that it overheats easily and to not place it on carpet - great advice, as I read that I looked across the room and saw I'd placed it on the carpet! (power off of course, I haven't turned it on yet)
 

 Question - any of you have a good resource for price guides for components, or is the only option to monitor auctions on eBay for a while and figure out what goes for what. I found that "game charting" webpage that tells you what old games sell for, and it includes Atari, INTV, and Odyssey2, but no Channel F or Astrocade (nor RCA Studio, lol). I joke about the RCA, but actually I'm obsessed with that one and need to acquire it. Why? Well, there's a reason why people watch Plan 9 From Outer Space and Showgirls. And it aint for the graphics!
 

 Anyways, I want to thank Adam who's already been a help, and look forward to meeting the rest of you and hearing your input and advice. On anything and everything in this area - games, maintanence peripherals, BASIC - obviously I'm not a programmer but I'm psyched to get MP3 user made programs and see what's out there! 
 

 Jason

Ah, thank you for the correction, Michael. I guess you're right, I was defaulting to Astrocade. And I also had noticed the lid and wondered if it was the original one that came with it or not as well, thanks for that link! OK, I guess I was backwards on one thing though - I thought the white ones were the mail-order, and that the black ones were the first retail models. But you're saying I've got that opposite? 

 Wow, Michael - just checked out the first link - you know, I guess in my research I had seen the blue sticker on pics of early units, but I certainly didn't realize how many sticker variations there were, so it didn't register how early/rare that might be! The lid does have some scuffs. But no cracks. I've even wondered if the scuffs could be buffed out; they're not really scratches as smooth abrasions. 
 

 OK, and since you brought up the label - I'd already been planing on doing a write-up on just the name(changes) alone, and man is that history of labels a key example of this. I'm new here, so I hope I'm not speaking out of turn saying something critical, but the branding/marketing of this... I'm at a loss, it seems to be one of the worst in console history. All that change, I just have to think it was a major obstacle on building a consistent brand that could grow. But hey, that's just IMHO. And it's part of what makes console history interesting. It's a real shame the system didn't take off better, I would have loved to have traded in my Atari for Bally's superior tech. But I don't think I even heard of it, I just don't recall. I had friends with INTV, Atari 5200, Colecovision, and I think I played an Odyssey2 once or twice, probably demo units at a department store. 


 I was a mall rat when I was a kid, my mom worked at a dept. store and she'd take me to the mall and I'd just run wild by myself. You know, the kind of thing that'd get me taken away by CPS today, lol. I knew the sales clerks at the electronics department of my mom's store (she worked in housewares); they almost always had mainly or exclusivley Atari, so whenever I saw another console on demo I would pounce. 
 

 But I can't say I had heard of Fairchild, Bally, RCA - back in the day, just more recently in doing research. I actually saw the RCA on eBay 10 years ago, I was looking for a 70s pong console on a lark, and it kept popping up, so I thought it was another pong console. I didn't buy it because of the terrible looking controls, but it wasn't until the last year when researching that I realized what I'd almost bought. 
 

 Oh, one more note - I can't play it yet (and maybe never), but I messed around with the controllers, and I'm LOVING the design. It's like they took the Fairchild and made it better by taking one control out of the joystick mechanism. The jerking motion of the Fairchild's firing can affect your movement control, so moving it to the trigger is an interesting idea.

Oh, wow - I don't see any red, take a look at this pic - is that where you mean it is? I guess it's an HLC. Does anyone know what "library" means or what the marketing message was? I get 'computer', but library seems weird to me, confusing.  

 Paul, I am thinking of not removing the shielding. Someone else recommended that and I install heat sinks. My understanding of the Bally Label changes.

The Original "Bally/Home Library Computer" was advertised as a Computer you would want in your home's library.

(I believe my Dad had a marketing flyer depicting that, but haven't seen one since. Just this JS&A flyer http://www.glankonian.com/~lance/Oba1.html

I believe Adam/BallyAlley has a colour version somewhere. :) )

The Keyboard expansion was intended to arrive a few months after the initial release.

During the 1977 launch, there was a change in management and the first label change.

There were actually 2 labels now. "Bally/Professional Arcade" for the game unit and "Bally/Computer System" Seen in all the promos for the Keyboard units on White systems.

http://www.glankonian.com/~lance/bally/OriginalKeyboard.jpg

The White units and the "Bally/Computer system" labels were not released until late in Bally's handling of the system. Even then not necessarily together.

When Astrovision took over the Home division for Bally, they mostly used the "Bally/Computer System" label and included the new Astro-BASIC cart with the system.

The agreement between Astrovision & Bally only allowed Astrovision to use the Bally logo for a limited time.

Astrovision originally intended to change the name of the system to "Astro/Professional Arcade" However, after making the labels and marketing, they were made aware of a previous Trademark owner of the Astrovision name in the video electronics market, so had to change their name. If there was a similar issue with the 'Astro' name for the system is unclear.

So, they scrapped that label, changed their name to Astrocade and the system to "Astrocade/The Professional Arcade". The quick change in brand/labelling explains the 2 style variations of "Astrocade" used.

Unfortunately, the loss of $ on labels and marketing for the 'Astro' hurt them and they when back to there existing stock of "Bally|Computer System" Labels inside the Astrocade boxes.

More on the keyboard(s) here:
http://www.glankonian.com/~lance/Z-Grass.html

And the arcade ports - those are key in a way that Star wars isn't (well, lol - except for Star Wars arcade ports - i mean star wars games original to the console) - ports of arcade games are key to consoles in supplying content, especially in the early days when there were less developers and/or no third party developers. 
 

 I had thought that perhaps, as far as home consoles - Superman (1978) was the first licensed game. Hey guys, I hope I'm not annoying everyone with tons of posts. I've just had so many Bally questions (well, retro in general) as I've been learning, and now that I've been joining these forums and groups they're kind of bubbling out. 
 

 But I was curious - I am not sure that I've even seen it mentioned in any of the coverage I've seen and read on Bally - that the console bears a striking resemblance to the physical design of the Channel F. I mean intensely striking. To the point of not being comprehensible that it could be a coincidence. The plastic lid. The angular trapezoid shape. Cartridge location in near-identical positioning. The same (or practically) JOYSTICK CONTROLLERS!!!! I mean, those were pretty damn unique - easy to spot a knock-off there. 
 

 Now, not that I'm saying this is bad or good or whatever, I'm not sure. I'm interested to hear what you think, if this has come up before (keep in mind what may be new to me could be boringly old hat to you, if so - apoligies!). Has anyone at Bally's ever commented on that? I wonder. 
 

 I mean, there are differences, no doubt. Some pretty peripheral - Channel F looks deeper, storage section originated in opposites between them. But there are a couple changes that are interesting. Obviously adding the keypad is a functional improvement. But the cartridges - cassette over 8 track. VERY interesting. Fairchild went with 8-Track - in music, 8-Track was higher quality, but older tech, lacking in some features (no rewind, for example), something familiar to a consumer that has never heard of "game cartridges" before. Using a delivery shape reminiscent of one of music industry kind of helps establish it as an entity of IP, another thing to play - on your 8-Track, on your Fairchild. And it's older tech- familiar to the audience, comfortable. A good strategy - by Nick Talesfor - especially for the first ever console. 
 

 Conversely, Astrocade went also for the music model, but instead choosing the next medium, audio cassette tapes. A stark contrast to the Fairchild. In music, cassette is lower quality audio (though obviously that's moot in the game version, as obviously it was just shapes of cartridges). But it was the future, 8-Tracks were dying. Plus, if we consider Bally's year of entry into the market 1978 - as it was what, January '78 that they first started actually delivering units that they had sold in 77, right? I bet Lance would be able to confirm or disconfirm that. Anyways, if it's '78 - that means that Bally is coming out demonstrably later than Fairchild, the first Christmas shopping season they were in stores was end of 78. By then, Bally would be the fourth cartridge based console on the market. Thus, that feeling of familiarity and comfort of the 8-track - which was having diminishing returns as 8-Tracks faded - would perhaps be better to be replaced by that symbol of the future, the cassette, which was only going to be getting bigger in the years to come. 
 

 So I guess in a strange way, I'm saying that both of these approaches were very interesting and I think good examples of design for their respective reasons. And both were probably the right decision, for each of the consoles and the time they hit the market. 
 

 Another adjustment to the Fairchild design is that Bally is not as deep and is it a little taller? Haven't seen Channel F in person, but the angular shape of the front on the Bally - whether it's taller or not, the angles appear to me to be at sharper degrees. It's different from Fairchild, but in the direction of more extreme. As opposed to what the Fairchild migrated to, a design softening those angles in the System II.
 

 And of course the controllers - adding trigger - first pistol grip trigger controller? (triggers on light guns don't count in this category)
 

 That was eating at me for a while, so thank you if you made it all the through for indulging me in some questions and thoughts on these two fine bits of console history.
 

 Jason

Ah, no.

I was just appending the Company name for clarification.

"Bally | Home Library Computer" is made by Bally
"Bally | Professional Arcade" is made by Bally
"Bally | Computer System" is made by Bally
Astrovision inc. buys home division from Bally
BPA/BCS now Sold by Astrovision & allowed to use the Bally name temporarily.
Astrovision gears up for change to "Astro | Professional Arcade"
Legal stuff happens...
Astrovision becomes Astrocade Inc. System label becomes the "Astrocade".'The professional Arcade' is all smaller case on label.

When I went to the stores where this system was available, everyone just called it the Bally or Bally home system.

When it changed to Astrocade it was already very hard to find in my area.

I usually either just call it Bally or Bally/Astrocade. In my case I'm noting the first & last Co. to sell it.

Some people just call it the Astrocade, but people who only see Bally labelled units may be confused.

Lance

I logged onto my email this morning to check if our newest Yahoo group member posted anything to the board.  It sure looks like it!  I see many, many posts.  I'm going out of town today and won't have time to read them over, so I'll check these out tomorrow night or Monday morning.  I hope that he's getting the help that he needs (this is the place to ask, right?).  Once someone starts a topic on this group, then many people respond.

One last thing about the Yahoo group I should mention to all new members (and I probably should have before).  Sometimes there is quite a delay from when a message is posted to the group, to when it actually shows up.  Sometimes a post goes up instantly, and sometimes it lags around for a day (or even two), but it will eventually show up.  Sometimes people double, triple, or even quadruple post.  Hopefully that's not what is happening.  I guess I'll find out when I read the messages.

Since "4cade1" has free time before his real Astrocade is (hopefully) running, then he should try to set-up the MESS emulator.  There are plenty of people on this board that can help him with out.  All of the Astrocade ROMs to play with it are here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/cart_images/cart_images.html

This set includes all of the released and prototype carts, as well as BASICarts (tape games that have been converted to run as cartridges).  Not all games will work with MESS, as the Bally Arcade has the ability to load a game, go into a loop, switch-out carts, and then put in the BASIC (or any other cart) and then start running again.  It's the only system I know that can do it (although I'm not sure if it's unique ONLY to the Astrocade), but the MESS emulator doesn't support this cart-swapping property.

Adam

(note - I deleted and re-posted this because I used the wrong game name in one part which was confusing): 

 Yeah, Paul - I thought the same thing about arcade ports. It's a little hard to research because most sources don't categorize it by that way - however, in the earliest part of vid game history, it's a little easier. The consoles are finite, and many of them have no (officially) licensed games of any kind. That's one reason why I don't focus much on computer games - it's more outside my wheelhouse and there are so many different computer systems that to track each one down and review it's game library for comparison is really tough, at least for me anyways. i'm sure there's some out there who's a bigger man than I and would tackle that. 

 And you make another good point - RELEASE DATES. I have been so frustrated at the lack of info on that. Fairchild specifically, very hard to find release dates for the games, at least in my experience so far. Wiki and others give year dates for Astrocade, However - in this case, I think we can be more certain. Bally had Gunfight as a built in game - if they shipped their first units in Jan/78, then we can say that date for sure, I think. Some may say "they sold it in late 77 I'll count that as the date" or not, but I am assuming if they shipped on 1/78 we can count that. 
 

 It doesn't appear Atari has any arcade ports in the first two years of their game library (77 & 78). So who else was out in January 1978 - Fairchild, RCA - neither of which had any officially licensed games. It seems as through process of elmination we can safely say that Gunfight is the first, and it must be an official release, as it uses the name and was a Midway (subsidiary of Bally) game. 
 

 Yes, Paul - Phaser Strike is on the list! However - for a certain reason. This article isn't about official Trek/Wars games, but unofficial - and while this was the first official game, when they continued the game withOUT the Trek license, I feel it qualifies for this list! (and I would bet you can imagine another game on the list that had the same situation Phaser Strike did) 
 

 I'll give you a clue as to another on this list - a clue of course I'm sure no one on this list would need me to suggest, but Star Battle for the Astrocade. Need I go into why?

13681:
Oh my gosh, you are totally right, Bill. First off, since Atari was an arcade company, of course their porting their stuff - so I should've looked into their early arcade games, I do not believe I've ever heard of Starship 1, let alone played it. But I had Star Ship 2600 at launch, but I was pretty young, maybe that arcade game was a little before my time (but I would often find/play other older units, I think I've played Space Wars, that only came out a year later). 

 I just looked up some video on this - OMG... this totally changes my perspective. You know how long I played 2600 Star Ship before I realized that the enemy 'ship' was just that, a saucer section and nacelles - instead of what I saw it as, an off kilter "O" and "Z" overlapping each other, ominously approaching me. I was just getting used to Trek from it airing in syndication,and it was a while before I could see it as a ship.
 

 But when I saw the arcade version - totally makes sense now. They do have a ship that looks like the Klingon BoP too in the arcade. 
 

 OK, I've now checked out vids on the rest. Of course, you're right about all of them. Indy 800, up to 8 people, I remember that one, but very vaguely. Tank - I bet I played that once or twice, but again would be as a lark, as it would have been one of the 'older' machines if i was arcading in the early 80s. 
 

 You know, I think Combat is one of the best games of Gen2 home consoles, especially if you consider how early it came out. I played a lot of Atari games over the years where literally within 30 seconds, it was repetitive. But I logged serious hours on that, albeit much fighting (or getting killed) by my brothers. And the gameplay variations - which up to the late 70s had almost been a 'scam', as many consoles promised dozens of games only to have the kids start playing and realizing it's all just pong. The variations on Combat were great.I bet you that I played Tank once or twice but it actually seemed primitive to the Atari version (except for those awesome double-joystick controllers in the arcade), and I'm not surprised I would've forgotten about that one. 
 

 Bill, thank you for the info, I really appreciate it. I was writing down some notes on the console wars the other day and I thought that one of the things that made it more challenging for most of Atari's competitors, is that they were more coming from the place of being a hardware manufacturer, whereas Atari did some of that but was more of a game developer, which gave their games a huge advantage when Atari hit the market. I thought that because Atari's launch games were A) a pretty high number for a launch, like 9 games?, and B) I think several of them are really good, a high % for launch games of that era. But your point that so many launch games came directly from their previous arcade work, yeah that totally strengthens that point, I'm glad you chimed in.

I own a Bally Professional Arcade. 
Bought as untested, but 6 controllers and 25+ games spoke to me that this worked good and was used and enjoyed and invested in buying all those games. 

Upon first hook up it was snowy and barely visible. 
Removing the "switch box" and putting an adapter on the RF cable (so it looks like the coax cable from the cable company) it is perfect!
If your display has a coax cable input, and not just the antenna screws, get one of those adapters on AtariAge or ebay or ask at a local store for RCA to Coax adapter.
If your TV has a menu, make sure cable input is set to antenna and try channels 2, 3 & 4. 

Advanced skill level:
I have removed the RF shield, installed 3 heat sinks on the large IC chips with white thermal paste compound and epoxy, added a tiny fan from a broken Mac Mini powered off the light pen voltage. Replaced the one large capacitor because the original had a spot of corrosion where the wire enters the cylinder. (Cap kit from Console5.com)

Well, I'm not suggesting we rat out Esoterica to Paramount Pictures, or anything. :) Of course, from a legal perspective, it's not really any different. Small as they were, many of the games I mentioned were commercial products--advertised in newsletters and sold for a profit.
The gameplay depends on which one you're talking about. But I recall many games like that being simple, text-based resource management games. For example, you might engage in battles while managing your shields, phasers, and photon torpedoes.
Bally BASIC is a unique version of Tiny BASIC. So these won't run on a PC as is, but would probably be relatively easy to convert if someone were so inclined. You can, however, load them from a PC into an Astrocade by running a cable from your sound card to the appropriate Astrocade interface. The 2000 baud recordings use an interface directly in the cart, while the 300 baud recordings require an external interface that plugs into the light pen port. In either case, the PC is simply serving the same function as a cassette player would have originally.
Paul

Paul - I figured why beat around the bush - I may as well run this list by the group and see what people think. Most of them basically are using Wars/Trek ship designs, and I'm sure you'll be familiar with most/all. The thing is, Trek/Wars have among the most distinctive ship designs in sci-fi, so it was pretty easy - Ties, X-Wings, and ships with nacelles and saucer sections (and many of them coincide directly with the film releases).
 

 I don't think most of them are surprising necessarily, but compiled into one list (which I've not yet seen), it kinda is. I also found a handful that are basically doing the trench scene finale from Wars. 
 

 The finale - the most obscure! This one's for you, Bill - the RCA Studio II game Space War was re-titled to Star Wars after the release of the movie. Well, re-titled to Star Wars - in Europe. I saw it listed on Wiki but was skeptical until some guy posted a pic of the Sheen M1200 Star Wars game, and Sheen is wha RCA was called in Europe and Australia, I believe. OK, here's the list, not necessarily in order:
 

 Fairchild Channel F - Galactic Space War - enemies look like Enterprise and kind of like Klingon BoP
 1.       Atari 2600 - Vanguard - Atari 2600 - Theme music variation on SW
 2.       Space Wars Arcade (1977 Arcade) -Ship is clearly EnterpriseF
 3.       Odyssey 2 - Cosmic Conflict! - Standard FPS space, but Tie-Fighter enemies
 4.       Intellivision - Space Spartan (1982) - Darth Vader's curved Tie
 5.       Intellivision - Battle of Hoth - Homebrew (may not be included, but boy is it cool)
 6.       Megamania - Activision - Star Trek Enterprise style ship
 7.       Atari 2600 - Star Ship - Blob that looks like side view of enterprise
 8.       Atari 2600 - Challenge of Nexar - Tie Fighter enemies
 9.       Atari 2600 - Space Canyon (1983) - Your ship looks like USS Reliant
 10.   Atari 2600 - Galaxian - 2600 Port - Your ship has nacelles
 11.   Atari 2600 - Starmaster  (1982) - Enemy with nacelles like Klingon Bird of Prey
 12.   Atari 2600 - Star Raiders (1982) Rips off 3 sci-fi franchises! Ties, Klingon BoP, Cylon Basestar, and opening music sounds like Close Encounters
 13.   Atari 2600 - Encounter at L5 - Ship has nacelles
 14.   Atari 2600 - Star Voyager - enemy looks like Klingon BoP
 15.   Microvision - Star Trek: Phaser Strike (1979) 
 16.   Vectrex - Star Trek - sold without Trek license as well
 17.   Astrocade - Star Battle (1978) - Star Wars trench scene w/X-Wing & Tie Fighter
 18.   Intellivision- Star Strike (1982) - SW trench scene (ships not done SW style), planet targeted
 19.   Vectrex - Star Hawk (1982) - Loosely looks like SW trench scene
 20.   RCA - Space War (1977) - Foreign release in Fr/Aus as Star Wars

13691:
That is a great game of "Space Fortress."  The controller works very well for this game.

I'm glad to hear that the Astrocade was popular at the expo.  Most people haven't seen one, so it's pretty unusual-- and many people seem surprised at what it is capable of doing.

Were you able to share a few games using BASIC at the expo?  Even people who own working systems usually don't see these kinds of games.  Sure, they're written in BASIC: the colors are limited and the gameplay can be slow, but there are BASIC games that would never have made it into cartridge format.  Also, the Bally Arcade/Astrocade community kept their system going in the late 70s and early 80s with those games on tape and type-in listing available in the newsletters.  It's also neat that "Artillery Duel," originally a BASIC game published in "The Arcadian" (and later in the AstroBASIC manual) later became a cartridge.

I hope that a wonderful game of "Dog Patch" was played at the expo too; it's a fun game.  Two good players can make the game amazing to watch.  Two not-so-good players will find the game boring and nobody would be interested in watching a game of that.  Give the game a go at the next gather that you attend.

Adam

A "Space Zap" / "Space Fortress" clone was made for AstroBASIC and published in the "Arcadian" newsletter.  This game, by George Moses, was called "Astro Zap 2000."  It was released via these methods:

1) Tape SB-G15 - Included as an extra or bonus program

http://www.ballyalley.com/ads_and_catalogs/George%20Moses%20Software%20%28Ad%29%28Programs%20A-E%29.pdf

2) ARCADIAN 4, no. 9 (Jul. 06, 1982): 88. - $100 prize winner this month.

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_4/arcadian_vol_4_issue_09.pdf#page=4

3) Vol. 4, Pg. 88, Arcadian, Vol. 6, Pg. 89 (Reprint)

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_6/arcadian_vol_6_issue_10.pdf#page=1

The AstroBASIC version can be download here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/george_moses/games/Astro%20Zap%202000%20(George%20Moses).zip

"Astro Zap 2000" was translated to Blue Ram BASIC, but it didn't have an official release.  The BRB version can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/ram_expansion_required/programs_a-h/Astro%20Zap%20(George%20Moses)(BRB).zip

I've played this game, and it plays pretty well.  Give it a try; you'll like it.

An Astrocade podcast (with probably two other hosts) will be starting soon.  It will likely be called "The Bally Alley Astrocast."  My son, a college senior who is majoring in music education, is interested in making the intro music for it.  It will be short (perhaps about 20 or 30 seconds long).  I'm pretty-open to his ideas, be they for flute (his primary instrument), electronic (created using, probably, FL Studio), or music composed of Astrocade sound-effects.  I'm sure it will be fine if it suits his fancy.  He composed wonderfully.

There are not many games that have music in them for the Astrocade, although a few do have tunes or neat sound effects.  He needs help with a few the following suggestions:

1) The melody of a song (or songs) from a better-known Astrocade game.

2) Popular Astrocade sound effects, or maybe even sound effects from an arcade game based on the Astrocade chipset.

3) Videos of 3 or 4 Astrocade games that have melodies that might be catchy or otherwise memorable.

(Since Astrocade videos are scarce, if someone can name some music or effects that they like, I can record it for him using my setup.)

What do music/sound effects can you name that if you heard it, you would think "Oh, it's the Astrocade."?

Brett Bilbrey wrote:
>>

As I suspected, YouTube doesn't have any video for this 1978 cartridge.  I did record this music from the cart quite a few years ago.  It's here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/audio/Music_%28From_Carts%29/Music%20%28Bally%20Pro%20Arcade%20Demo%20Cart%29.mp3

I'm pretty sure that this was a theme-song used by Commodore or Texas Instruments.  Does anyone know for sure?  Can someone point out an example if you do remember where it is from exactly?

The song from the Bally Demo cart is one of Bach's two-part inventions, right?  If so, then it is probably on the Bach tape by that George Moses released.  All fifteen of the songs for that music is available to listen to here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/audio/george_moses/Bach's_15_Two-Part_Inventions_%5BTape_1%5D/two-part_inventions.html

I also suggested to my son that he might check-out the entire audio area of BallyAlley for inspiration too:

http://www.ballyalley.com/audio/audio.html

I have always wanted to add more sound-effects and music from more Astrocade cartridges to the audio area, but it's a time-consuming process that I never did re-visit.

I like the audio chip in the Bally Arcade.  It seems to be better than most of the sound chips in any of the home consoles in 1977/78.  Maybe it was even better than most computers until the Atari 400/800 was released in November 1979 in limited numbers.  Any thoughts on this?  How did it stack up against competitors when the Astrocade was re-released?

Whatever my son creates for the theme song, it will be better music than what was used in this awful C64 commercial:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PMmeNaFuVUM

Any other suggestions for Bally podcast theme music?

Here is the Astrocade podcast music:

https://soundcloud.com/chilaxicle/astrocast-intro

I started just by looking through your emails for a sound effect that I thought would work well. I liked the "New Candy Man" sound effect from Candy Man so used that for the song.  The five recorded sound effects  for "Candy Man" by L&M Software played on a real Astrocade can be downloaded here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/audio/Sound_Effects_%28From_Tape_Games%29/sound_effects.html

I listened to the sound effect a few times and tried to play something along with it on my flute that fit to me. After getting the first couple of measures and feeling satisfied with them, I wrote them down in Finale using my piano. After that wrote the rest just on flute, writing it down as I went along. Once that was finished, I added chords on piano, and found a rhythm for it that I thought fit nicely. Once those were in place, the bass almost wrote itself.  I learned how to write basic bass parts in my Jazz Pedagogy class it and really helped out. The sheet music that I wrote for it is available here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/audio/Music_%28Various_Authors%29/various_authors.html#AstrocastTheme

At this point I saved the Finale as a MIDI and opened it in FL Studio. I deleted the flute part, since I was going to record live, and opened up my favorite piano VST for the piano. I ended up using what I think is a nice warm piano sound. For the bass I took a soundfont that comes with FL Studio and changed it both on the synthesizer itself and by running it through an EQ. Once I could loop that, I took takes on my flute until I got one that sounded right to me.

I had already contacted Brandon (who lives in another state), so Sunday afternoon I sent it off to him to add drums. I gave him a few instructions on how to start and end the piece, but left everything else up to him. He finished it just about an hour ago, and sent me his drums with my part and just his drums alone. I took his drums and ran it through an EQ in FL Studio so it would blend a little nicer, and called it done!

- Dominic Lowhar

I doubt that a black screen on start-up is caused by a problem as simple as a loose RF cable on the Astrocade.  I suppose that it can't hurt to check it, but even a black screen means that the TV is getting a signal of some sort.

The cartridge runs about four minutes (continuous loop) and features the "built in" software of the Bally console.  Written by Dick Ainsworth.
(Arcadian vol.4 pg.11,44,84,124, vol.5 pg.97,115,123,139,vol.6 pg.5,27,34,35,44,45,63,71, Niagara Bug Bulletin vol.1 pg.17, vol.2 pg.3)

This information is from "Bally-Astrocade Game Cartridge and Hardware FAQ" by Paul Thacker, Adam Trionfo and Mike White.  It can be read, here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/astrocade_cart_and_hardware_faq.txt

That should help you out.  The more interesting of the two demo cart for the Bally Arcade/Astrocade is the "Bally BASIC Demo" cart.  Here is some information about the BASIC Demo cart from the above FAQ:

Bally BASIC Demo
     Bally Mfg. Corp.  Functional Series              8K cart  1978.
This cartridge has a small (about 6") chain attached to the top-front. This cartridge was made in limited quantities and only distributed to dealers, as was also done with the Dealer Demo cartridge. This 8K cartridge ( a rarity in the old days) is very hard to find, but has appeared on eBay. The first 4K is a "crippled" version of Bally BASIC that doesn't have access to the
keypad or hand controllers- except #3: all the inputs are disabled. The remaining 4K of the cartridge is a program written in BASIC! This was in 1978, EIGHT YEARS before Basicarts appeared! This cartridge may have sometimes been accompanied by a 300 Baud Demo Interface. This cartridge might be #6003 (it fits there), but there is no proof of this part number assignment. (Arcadian vol.1 pg.46)

Here is a picture of the "Bally BASIC Demo" cart:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/cartridge_pics/Carts_%28Astrocade-Bally%29/full_size/Bally_BASIC_Demo-%28With_Chain%29.jpg

Enjoy the Dealer Demo cart.  Even if the Demo cart only shows the built-in software, it's still pretty neat.  Try running it in the MESS Astrocade emulator.

Adam

Yesterday I got "Dragon Naturally Speaking" for several reasons related to archiving and podcasting.  As a test, I thought that it might be fun to dictate a hand-written letter that was written to the "Arcadian" newsletter by Brett Bilbrey back in 1980.  The original letter is five pages long, but it seems much short once you see the "typed" version of it.  I have less than an hour's worth of experience with "Dragon," and yet I was able to dictate and edit this letter in about fifteen minutes.  I'd say my test of "Dragon" was very successful.

@Brett (who is a member of this Bally Alley group): Do you have any comments about this letter from 35 years ago?  Does it bring back any memories?

Enjoy this nearly lost piece of videogame/computer history.

Adam


11-5-80

Dear Mr. Fabris,

As you know we had a rather successful users group meeting here in Michigan.  Mr. Moses has informed me that he has kept you informed as to what has happened.

Mr. Cornett has included some articles in his newsletter that were "written" by me.  Well that's close.  I sent him some articles and he rewrote them.  I give credit to your newsletter for details on the Critter, but he did not print that (of course).  The only reason I sent that to him was to show what could be done with adding memory could be done with just BASIC.  He never mentioned that.  Also, I sent him a short tutorial on the I/O ports that pertain to the foreground/background process, and he turns around and makes it into a "Peek N' Poke" manual.  And to top it off, he does not even tell me!

Well, I know that Mr. Perkins is as capable or more so than I, and that FAST ACTION GRAPHICS article (of his?) shows that you have good programmers behind you.  That is why I am continuing to subscribe to your newsletter.  It's good, no matter what others say!

Some news and good news:
I have received some information directly from Dave Nutting Associates regarding HIGH Resolution Screen Display.  We can get high resolution, but it requires the addition of 12K of ROM and some hardware modifications to the game.  We are working out all the details now and should have an announcement letter about this.

Also, more good news from Mr. Anderson.  He may have found the answer for the Light Pen.  He claims that a very low cost Light Pen will be forthcoming from him. (Yeah Team!)  I have already started on this topic and have a great deal of information on how to use a light pen with respect to programming, if you're interested.  Please let me know.

I have started a partnership with three friends, it's called SPECTRE Systems.  Right now we have limited our sales to TRS-80 software (large market), but we hope to expand to produce professional BALLY cartridges.  Something like Activision did for Atari.

We hope to expand our user's group and develop a more professional approach to the next meeting.  We will have discussion groups, guest lectures from Dave Nutting Associates, Bally and Astrovision, and some questionnaires as to what users are interested in and would like to see (including what type of ADD-ON).  We are lucky to be so close to both Dave Nutting Associates and Astrovision.

We are planning our next meeting for January.  Please let everyone know that if they're interested in attending our next users group, we would like to have them call either

     Brett Bilbrey [Number Excluded Here]
or   George Moses  [Number Excluded Here]

for more information and details.  Perhaps even some of our friends on the West Coast would like to come out and join us?  If there was enough interest we could make it a two or three day seminar.  I've included a copy of the program I sent to Mr. Cornett.  It explains how the machine listing and basic program relate.  This is designed to run on the BALLY BASIC without added memory.  It is a good example of machine language programming using the interrupt service routine and vector writing and moving.  (It shows what the mnemonics are for machine op-codes.)

I hope to soon be developing even more interesting things for the Bally.  (Light pen software, hi-res, cartridges...)

Please write if you have any information for our user's group.

Sincerely,
Brett Bilbrey

13728:
In the early days of the Bally Alley Yahoo discussion group there was a frequent contributor named Tony Miller.  He helped to design the Bally Arcade computer expansion that went unreleased in 1978.  I thought it would be a good idea to interview him for an upcoming episode of the Astrocast podcast.  I looked him up on the Internet and I didn't have any trouble finding, I think, his website:

http://www.west.net/~jay/fmillera/fmillera/

Tony's site is dedicated to jukeboxes, but under his list of accomplishments, Tony says that he helped create the unreleased computer add-on for the Bally Arcade.  This accomplishment fits "our" Tony Miller perfectly.  Sadly, shortly afterward, I found a post by "KenLayton" in a Jukebox collecting forum that gave unexpected news:

"It is with great sadness to report that Seeburg juke box expert Tony Miller passed away suddenly on Monday April 6, 2009."

You can see "KenLayton's" original post, here:

http://forums.arcade-museum.com/archive/index.php/t-86603.html

I privately asked several members of this Bally Alley discussion group if they had heard anything about this before.  Paul Thacker investigated past messages posted to the Yahoo group messages and discovered that "the last post [...] from Tony [was] on March 15, 2009."  This is about three weeks before the forum post says that Tony died.

In the early days of this discussion group (about 2001), there was talk of just how easy it might be to upgrade the Astrocade to hi-res mode.  Tony Miller insisted that it wasn't as easy as people expected.  Yet, still the rumor persisted (and in some ways, it still does to this day).  In 2001, Tony seemed to have reached a personal boiling point about this supposed easy-to-make hi-res unit that people dreamed about creating.  Tony used his creative energy to write a 25-page description of the Bally Professional Arcade Video Hardware and Associated Coin-Operated Hardware.  This description proved to Tony's satisfaction that the commercial (high-resolution) mode of the Astrocade was not possible with a simple RAM upgrade.  Tony's  discussion of the video hardware can be read here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/bally_professional_arcade_video_hardware_faq.zip

Although I didn't know Tony personally (we never spoke), it was Tony's dedication to details in the Bally community (and, from what I see now, also in the jukebox collecting community) that brought me a particular heavy sadness when I discovered that he had died.  My heartfelt (though) late, condolences go out to his family.

If anyone on this group knew Tony, or know of his exploits, then I'd love to hear more about him and his technical and creative pursuits.

Adam

13734:
I added the a "Magic Register Tutorial" by Brett Bilbrey.  This was submitted to Bob Fabris in December 1981.  This is an update of an earlier tutorial that, I think, Brett also wrote.  I don't think that this update was ever published before in the Arcadian or Cursor newsletter.

You may be asking yourself just what is the Magic register?  On page 94 of the "Nutting Manual" it is described as "The Magic System is enabled when data is written to a memory location (X) from 0 to 16K. A modified form of the data is actually written in memory location X+16K. The magic register (output port $0C) determines how the data is modified."

In the included letter that Brett wrote to Bob Fabris, Brett notes that this four-page tutorial is a "better tutorial of the MAGIC register. Yes, the old MAGIC tutorial was working ok. It was just a bad example."

Although the article is aimed at users of Bally BASIC, I'm sure if your interests are more in tune with machine language, then you'll get something out of this too.

You can read the tutorial here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/Magic_Register_Tutorial_(Bilbrey)/Magic%20Register%20Tutorial%20(December%2010%201981)(Brett%20Bilbrey).pdf

Brett, did you discover all of this on your own-- or did you get the help of others in the Bally community?  Surely by 1981 you had access to the "Nutting Manual," right?

Adam
13735:
Adam, 

 To answer your question:
 Brett, did you discover all of this on your own-- or did you get the help of others in the Bally community?  Surely by 1981 you had access to the "Nutting Manual," right?

I did have access to the Nutting Manual by that time. 

 Before writing the various tutorials, I was learning about computers, software and 'firmware'. The Bally was a wonderful platform for me to use as a development environment. I liked the elegant architecture of the Z80 processor. It made understanding assembly programming pretty straight forward.
 

 At the same time, I was learning about IBM 360 programming at the University of Michigan, as well as learning about Electrical Engineering. The Bally was my 'testbed' that I could experiment with. It was fun learning about programming synchronization with video (that is, learning to draw to the screen so that the video did not 'flicker'), learning about color representation (That is, the difference between swapping out colors like I did for Treasure Cove and ICBM Attack, and color depth which would be a full 24 or 32 bit deep color representation), learning about sound effects and music (At UofM, for my 'intro to assembly programming class where we had to build a project that interfaced with the real world, I made a music player on a 6502 based PET computer, and had it play the UofM fight song.), and just learning how to access hardware from registers...
 

 It was a wonderful time of learning, exploring and having fun. I enjoyed sharing that with others via the tutorials. 
 

 Brett

13741:
I added a "GAME OVER Tutorial" by Tom Wood.  This was sent to the "Arcadian" on January 18, 1979.

This tutorial provides a machine language subroutine usable to BASIC users so that they can print "GAME OVER" in large letters on the screen using a subroutine that is built into the Bally's 8K System ROM. This tutorial was published in a much shorter format in the "Arcadian." In this expanded version, Mr. Wood provides more information on how the subroutine works and also explains why it won't work the same on all Bally Arcades due to slight differences in the System ROM.

http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/GAME_OVER_Tutorial/Tutorial%20(Tom%20Woods)(Jan%2018%201979)(Game%20Over).pdf

The typically 10-page "Arcadian" often edited articles for space reasons.  It would have benefited readers to have had entire articles printed, but editing for space did allow Bob Fabris to print more material.  Many users seemed to have dug into the tutorials and programs and learned as much as they could on their own.

Adam
13742:
I added "Random Numbers Tutorial" by Rich Tietjens.

This six-page, previously unpublished "Arcadian" submission, is a hand-written tutorial that covers the accuracy of using the RND statement to create random numbers in Bally BASIC. Three BASIC type-in programs are provided as examples for readers.

You can read the tutorial here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/Random_Numbers/Random%20Numbers%20(Rich%20Tietjens).pdf

This article is rather detailed and covers a topic I don't recall getting any coverage at all in the the Astrocade newsletters.  I can understand why it wasn't published, as it's appeal is rather limited-- yet the subject is quite interesting.  I'm glad that this article turned up in the Bob Fabris Archive, as it was a fun read and proves that users were interested in more than just the gaming aspects of the Bally Arcade-- although I bet Rich began looking into the subject to write games, but then he got caught-up in the material.

Adam

Since Craig Anderson chimed in today on the discussion group (it's always great to hear from old-timers!), I've added an article by him called "Tape Archival Storage and Basic Maintenance."  This was written August 5, 1980.  As far as I can tell, this was another article that was never published in its entirety.

This article was written as a cure-all for most of the problems related to loss of programs after a period of time which was mentioned briefly as "Tape Dropout???" in ARCADIAN 2, no. 9 (Jul. 28, 1980): 84.

In the article, Craig notes that "while the article is rather lengthy. It is critical to the owner of a computer with cassette storage, and since nothing has been published on the topic in either of the newsletters, it is certainly worth devoting considerable space to. You may feel free to edit and condense it to suit your space requirements." Parts of this article were probably published in the "Arcadian" to follow-up on the problems that some users were experiencing with tape storage.

http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/Tape_Archival_Storage/Tape%20Archival%20Storage%20and%20Basic%20Maintenance%20(August%201980)(ARD).pdf

Ask anyone under thirty years-old what tape storage is when using a computer.  See what sort of answer that you get from them.  I bet that it will be funny!

13746:
I added "Bally Arcade: More Than Fun" by Graham M Wideman and Mark J Czerwinski.

This is an article from the November 1978 issue of Electronics Today, a Canadian electronics enthusiast magazine. The article covers the Bally Arcade. Although the page numbers are not consecutive in this scan, the article is complete (full page advertisements were removed). The article is notable because it assumes a basic level of technical knowledge and includes photographs of the internals.

This article was originally scanned by BOXPRESSED in January 2014 and posted to his blog on RetroAuction.com. The person that scanned it asked me to give credit to the blog if the article was posted on BallyAlley.

The originally post said, "Hi friends. I recently acquired an old issue of Electronics Today (an electronics enthusiast magazine out of Canada) from 1978. Included is an article on the Bally Arcade, yet to be released in Canada at the time of the article's writing. I have scanned the article and uploaded it to my blog (link below). Enjoy!"

You can download the article here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/articles_and_news/Bally_Arcade-More_Than_Fun_(Nov_1978)/Bally%20Arcade%20-%20More%20Than%20Fun%20(Nov%201978)(Graham%20M%20Wideman%20and%20Mark%20J%20Czerwinski)%5BElectronics%20Today%5D.pdf

This article was discussed on the Yahoo group back in January of 2001, when it was first posted to the blog.
